name: CCAO-F Core Bank
description: 210 blueprint-weighted items written against the published CCAO-F exam guide and public Anthropic documentation. Item counts match the blueprint weights to within 0.2 points; all 30 objectives covered.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: Anthropic's prompting guidance states a "golden rule of clear prompting" that candidates can apply to any business prompt. What is it?

options.text: Keep every prompt under 200 words, on the basis that a shorter instruction is easier for the model to hold in focus.
State every constraint as a prohibition, so that the model has an explicit list of the behaviours it must avoid.
Show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task; if they would be confused, Claude will be too.
Include at least ten worked examples, so that the model can infer the pattern without being given any instructions.

items.explanation: Anthropic's prompting best practices state the golden rule as showing the prompt to a colleague with minimal context and asking them to follow it: if they would be confused, Claude will be too. The same page frames Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows, which is why the colleague test works.

rationales.A: No word ceiling is prescribed. The guidance is to be as precise as the task needs, not to hit an arbitrary length limit.
rationales.B: The documented lever is the opposite: tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do. Prohibition-only phrasing is listed as a weaker way to control output.
rationales.D: The documented count for examples is 3-5, and the quality criteria matter more than volume. Ten-plus examples is a stated near-miss, not the golden rule.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A recruiter wants Claude to draft candidate feedback notes in a consistent in-house format, and plans to paste in some worked examples alongside the instruction. How should she assemble those examples?

options.text: Include a single flawless example, on the assumption that any further examples would only dilute the pattern.
Include at least ten near-identical examples, so that the pattern she wants cannot possibly be misread.
Include the examples only after the question, and never before the instructions themselves.
Include 3-5 examples that are relevant, diverse, and wrapped in example tags.

items.explanation: Anthropic prescribes a specific count and three quality criteria: include 3-5 examples for best results, and make each one relevant (it mirrors the actual use case), diverse (it covers edge cases and varies enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns), and structured (wrapped in example tags, with multiple examples inside an examples tag).

rationales.A: One example under-specifies the task and cannot cover edge cases. The documented range starts at three.
rationales.B: This fails both the count and the diversity criterion. Near-identical examples are exactly what causes Claude to pick up unintended patterns.
rationales.C: Ordering guidance concerns long documents (data near the top, query at the end), not examples. No rule forbids examples before instructions.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A procurement officer at a housing association pastes three vendor contracts totalling roughly 40,000 tokens into a single prompt and asks Claude to compare their termination clauses. The answers keep drifting to irrelevant sections. How should the prompt be restructured?

options.text: Place the comparison question first, so that Claude knows what to look for before it starts reading the contracts.
Place all three contracts near the top of the prompt and put the comparison question at the end.
Split the contracts across 20 small chats, so that no single prompt ever exceeds a few thousand tokens.
Wrap the entire prompt in one instructions tag, so that Claude treats the whole thing as a single unit.

items.explanation: For inputs of roughly 20,000 tokens or more, Anthropic's documented ordering is long documents and data near the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions and examples. Anthropic notes that queries placed at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs.

rationales.A: This is the exact inversion of the documented rule and is a named exam trap. Question-first ordering is what the up-to-30-percent finding argues against at this input size.
rationales.C: Fragmenting the corpus destroys the cross-document comparison the analyst needs and is not the documented remedy for drift in long-context prompts.
rationales.D: Anthropic's XML guidance is to wrap each type of content in its own descriptive tag, nesting each document inside its own document tag. Collapsing everything into one tag removes those distinctions and does nothing about ordering.

items.objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
items.stem: An HR partner drafting policy notices keeps receiving bulleted markdown when the house standard for these notices is continuous prose. Their current instruction reads: "Do not use markdown. Never use bullet points. Avoid headings." Which revision is most likely to fix it?

options.text: "Do not use markdown under any circumstances, and never use bullet points or headings anywhere in the notice."
"Convert your bulleted draft into continuous prose before you show any of it to me."
"Compose your response as smoothly flowing prose paragraphs."
"Follow the house style guide for policy notices, which is published on our intranet."

items.explanation: Anthropic lists four output-format levers in order of effectiveness, and the first is to tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do, using precisely this prose-paragraph example. The same show-do-not-forbid principle is repeated in the Claude Opus 5 guidance, which notes that positive examples of the communication style you want tend to be more effective than instructions about what not to do.

rationales.A: This only intensifies the prohibition framing that is already failing. Restating a negative more forcefully is the documented weaker lever.
rationales.B: A post-hoc conversion step treats each output individually and still leaves the model generating the wrong format first. The documented lever steers the format from the outset.
rationales.D: Claude is described as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms; it cannot read an intranet page it has not been given, so the format still has to be stated in the prompt.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: Anthropic recommends supplying motivation alongside an instruction, for example writing "Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses since the engine will not know how to pronounce them" rather than simply "NEVER use ellipses." What is the stated rationale?

options.text: Longer instructions consume more of the context window, which makes the constraint harder for the model to lose track of.
Claude generalises from the explanation to related situations the instruction did not name.
Explanations satisfy a policy requirement that every constraint given to the model be justified in writing.
The explanation removes any need to state success criteria for the task, since the intent has already been conveyed.

items.explanation: Anthropic's stated rationale for explaining the why behind an instruction is that Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation, applying the underlying intent to cases the literal rule did not enumerate. This is presented as a general prompting practice, not a formatting-only trick.

rationales.A: Length is not the mechanism. Padding a prompt does not improve adherence; the explanation works because it conveys intent.
rationales.C: There is no such policy requirement. The recommendation is a quality technique, not a compliance rule.
rationales.D: Success criteria remain a documented prerequisite for prompt engineering. Explaining a constraint does not substitute for defining what a good output looks like.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A programme officer at an education charity is using Claude Opus 5 and sends a prompt that reads in full: "Summarise this and make it good." The summary is generic and misses the funder's priorities. Which TWO revisions are most likely to fix it? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Append "double-check your work and include a final verification step" to the end of the prompt.
Wrap the source material in XML tags and change nothing else at all about the request.
Supply the background as though instructing someone with no prior knowledge of the funder or the deliverable.
Repeat the phrase "make it good" three times, so as to reinforce the quality expectation.
State positively what the summary should contain and how it should be structured for the audience.
Cut the prompt down to a single short sentence, so that Claude is not distracted by any detail.

items.explanation: Anthropic's help centre lists including as much context as possible, pretending you are instructing someone with no background knowledge, as a primary remedy for a weak answer, and the best-practices page makes stating what to do (rather than a vague quality wish) the leading output-control lever. Together these turn an under-specified request into a directed one.

rationales.A: Claude Opus 5 verifies its own work without being told to. Anthropic documents that explicit verification instructions cause over-verification on this model and should be removed rather than added.
rationales.B: XML tags help Claude parse a prompt that mixes instructions, context, examples and inputs, but tagging alone supplies none of the missing background and defines none of the criteria.
rationales.D: Repetition adds no information. The problem is missing context and undefined criteria, not insufficient emphasis.
rationales.F: The documented remedy for a weak answer is more context, not less: the help centre tells you to include as much context as possible.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A bid writer's prompt runs background notes, three sample paragraphs, the actual request and a block of pasted client requirements together as continuous text. Claude keeps treating the sample paragraphs as instructions. What should the bid writer change?

options.text: Delete the sample paragraphs, on the basis that mixing examples with instructions is unsupported in a single prompt.
Convert the whole prompt into a single numbered list, so that every element becomes an explicit step to perform.
Move the request to the very start of the prompt, so that it is read before any of the other material.
Wrap each kind of content in its own descriptive XML tag, nesting tags where the content has a natural hierarchy.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously, especially when a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples and variable inputs, and that wrapping each type of content in its own tag reduces misinterpretation. The stated best practices are consistent, descriptive tag names and nesting when content has a natural hierarchy. Examples specifically belong in example tags, with multiple examples inside an examples tag.

rationales.A: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer output format, tone and structure. The documented fix is to mark them as examples, not to remove them.
rationales.B: Numbered sequential steps are documented for when the order or completeness of steps matters. They do not tell Claude which block is background, which is an example and which is the request.
rationales.C: For inputs of about 20,000 tokens or more the documented ordering is the opposite, long data first and the query last, and in any case ordering alone does not label the content types.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A freelance copywriter supports two clients with conflicting terminology and tone rules. She wants Claude to apply one client's glossary and voice when she is working on that client's deliverables, and not on the other's. Which personalisation layer fits the requirement?

options.text: Account-wide instructions for Claude, which apply across every conversation on her account.
A one-off note pasted at the top of each conversation, added as and when she remembers to do it.
Project instructions attached to a project created for that client engagement.
A skill enabled during those chats, on the assumption that a skill carries the client's glossary.

items.explanation: Claude's personalisation layers differ by scope: instructions set at account level are described as account-wide settings that apply to all of your conversations, while project instructions apply only to chats within that project. Scoping a client glossary and voice to a single engagement is exactly what project instructions are for.

rationales.A: Account-level instructions apply to all of her conversations, so the first client's rules would leak into the second client's work. This is the classic scope near-miss.
rationales.B: Manual re-pasting is not a personalisation feature at all, and it fails on any conversation she forgets.
rationales.D: The help centre describes skills as behaviours or expertise you activate on demand, not as a boundary tied to one engagement; project instructions are the layer documented as applying only to chats within that project.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A membership officer types "Create a campaign dashboard" and gets a bare, minimal result. What should he change to get a more ambitious one?

options.text: Explicitly request the above-and-beyond behaviour, for example asking for as many relevant features and interactions as possible.
Rely on the model to infer the level of ambition from context, since current models no longer need such modifiers.
Send the same request again in a second message, repeating it until the output grows in scope.
Ask for a minimal version first and then build it up over several turns, on the basis that a fully featured result cannot come from a single pass.

items.explanation: Anthropic states that if you want above-and-beyond behaviour you should explicitly request it rather than relying on the model to infer it from vague prompts, and gives exactly this worked example: instead of "Create an analytics dashboard", use "Create an analytics dashboard. Include as many relevant features and interactions as possible. Go beyond the basics to create a fully-featured implementation." Framing instructions with such modifiers is also listed under migration considerations.

rationales.B: The documented position is the opposite: ambition still has to be stated, and adding modifiers that encourage higher quality and detail is a named technique.
rationales.C: Repetition supplies no new information about what a fuller result should contain.
rationales.D: Anthropic's own example asks for a fully featured implementation in a single prompt, so no minimal-first ceiling is documented.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: An information governance officer at an NHS trust asks Claude to identify data-retention obligations across a 200-page regulatory bundle. The answers mix in unrelated sections and she cannot tell which passages drove each conclusion. Which decomposition step should she add?

options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the whole bundle to one page first, and then answer the question from that summary.
Ask Claude to wrap each document in document and document_content tags, then ask exactly the same question again.
Ask Claude to re-read the bundle twice and report only the obligations that appear in both of its passes.
Ask Claude to first extract every relevant passage into quote tags, then perform the analysis on those quotes.

items.explanation: Anthropic recommends grounding responses in quotes for long-document tasks: ask Claude to quote the relevant parts of the documents first, before carrying out its task, which helps it focus on the relevant content and ignore the rest of the document. It also gives the analyst a traceable link from conclusion back to source text.

rationales.A: Summarising first discards the specific clause language the analysis depends on and adds a lossy step before the real task.
rationales.B: Document and metadata tagging is documented for multidocument inputs, but on its own it neither focuses Claude on the relevant passages nor produces the traceable link she needs. Quote grounding is the step that does.
rationales.C: Repeat passes are not a documented technique and simply consume more tokens without focusing the model on the relevant content.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: Anthropic notes that with adaptive thinking and subagent orchestration Claude handles most multistep reasoning internally, so splitting a task into explicitly chained steps that you run one after another is no longer required for every complex request. In which TWO situations does Anthropic still document explicit chaining as useful? (Select TWO.)

options.text: When the request runs to more than one sentence.
When you need to inspect the intermediate output of each step.
When the desired output must be formatted as prose.
When you need to enforce a specific pipeline structure.
When the response would otherwise run longer than a page.

items.explanation: Anthropic states that with adaptive thinking and subagent orchestration Claude handles most multistep reasoning internally, and that explicit prompt chaining is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure. Those two conditions are the documented justification for splitting the work into separate steps.

rationales.A: Sentence count is not a decomposition trigger. Multi-sentence requests are routinely handled in a single turn.
rationales.C: Prose formatting is an output-format lever, not a reason to split a task into separate steps.
rationales.E: Response length is controlled by prompting for it explicitly, not by chaining separate steps.

items.objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
items.stem: A visitor experience team at a museum seeds an ideation session by pasting three sample concepts, all of which happen to be ticket-discount offers, and asks Claude for twenty more ideas. Every idea it returns is another ticket discount. What best explains the narrowing, and what should the team change?

options.text: The seed examples were not diverse, so Claude picked up an unintended pattern; vary them across the shapes of concept wanted.
Twenty ideas exceeds what one response can reasonably cover, so the request should be split into four separate prompts asking for five concepts each.
Three examples sits below the documented range, so the team should paste seven further discount offers before asking for any new concepts.
The model needs a higher effort setting before it will produce variety, so the team should raise effort and reissue the identical prompt unchanged.

items.explanation: Examples are documented as one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output format, tone and structure, which is why an unrepresentative example set steers so strongly. The diversity criterion states that examples should cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns. Three all-alike seeds are precisely that unintended pattern, so the fix is to vary the seeds across the kinds of idea wanted rather than to add more of the same.

rationales.B: Breadth is not limited by response capacity here. The ideas are narrow rather than truncated, and splitting the same seed set across four prompts would simply reproduce the same pattern four times over.
rationales.C: Three examples already sits inside the documented 3-5 range, and adding seven more of the same kind would reinforce the very pattern that is narrowing the output.
rationales.D: Effort governs how much the model thinks rather than what it draws on, so raising it leaves the unintended pattern in the seed examples entirely untouched.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: A service desk manager at a utilities provider is preparing a quarterly service review. Task 1 is to rewrite a single escalation policy document section by section, each edit depending on the previous one. Task 2 is to profile four regional queues independently, one report per region, with no shared state. Which allocation of the two tasks is most appropriate?

options.text: Delegate Task 1 to parallel subagents, and handle Task 2 directly in a single working thread.
Delegate both tasks to subagents, on the basis that delegation reduces effort in every case.
Handle Task 1 directly in one working thread; delegate Task 2 to parallel subagents.
Handle both tasks directly, since subagents cannot produce separate written reports at all.

items.explanation: The documented sample guidance is to use subagents when tasks can run in parallel, require isolated context, or involve independent workstreams that do not need to share state, and to work directly for simple tasks, sequential operations, single-file edits, or tasks where you need to maintain context across steps. The sequential dependent rewrite is direct work; the four independent regional reports are the parallel, isolated-context case.

rationales.A: This inverts the rule. Parallelising a sequence of dependent edits breaks the context continuity each edit relies on.
rationales.B: Delegation is not universally beneficial; the documentation names specific cases where working directly is preferred, and warns that Claude may already over-delegate.
rationales.D: Independent parallel workstreams producing separate outputs are precisely the documented subagent use case, so refusing to delegate Task 2 ignores the guidance.

sources.title: Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: Anthropic's sample guidance on subagent usage also lists the conditions under which Claude should work directly rather than delegating. Which TWO of the following appear on that work-directly list? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The work is a wide investigation spanning many independent areas.
The subtasks can run in parallel.
The subtasks require isolated context from one another.
The operations have to run in sequence.
The workstreams are independent and do not need to share state.
Context has to be maintained across the steps.

items.explanation: The documented sample instruction has two halves. Delegate when tasks can run in parallel, require isolated context, or involve independent workstreams that do not need to share state. Work directly for simple tasks, sequential operations, single-file edits, or tasks where you need to maintain context across steps. Sequential operations and maintaining context across steps are on the work-directly half.

rationales.A: A wide, genuinely independent investigation is the canonical delegation case, not a reason to work directly.
rationales.B: Parallelism is the first condition on the delegate half of the guidance.
rationales.C: Isolated context is the second condition on the delegate half of the guidance.
rationales.E: Independent workstreams that do not need to share state are the third condition on the delegate half of the guidance.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: Claude's help centre article on unhelpful answers lists four ordered remedies. Which of the following is one of them, and is the one that corresponds directly to task decomposition?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window.
Break down complex requests into substeps.
Add three worked examples of the output you want.
Wrap the request in XML tags so Claude can parse it.

items.explanation: The four ordered remedies in the help centre article are: explain your ask simply and clearly; include as much context as possible; break down complex requests into substeps; and give Claude feedback through follow-up instructions, clarifications, or a request to rewrite an answer. The third of these is the decomposition remedy.

rationales.A: Model or context-window selection is not one of the four listed remedies for a weak answer.
rationales.C: Worked examples are a best-practices technique for steering format, tone and structure. They are not one of the four remedies in this article.
rationales.D: XML structuring is a best-practices technique for prompts that mix content types. It is not one of the four remedies in this article.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: A quality assurance lead at a rail operator is reviewing incident write-ups with Claude Opus 5 and instructs it to "only report high-severity issues and be conservative." The reviews come back very thin, and she later finds real medium-severity issues that were never surfaced. What should she change?

options.text: Restate the severity threshold more forcefully, so that the model applies it with greater care on each write-up.
Add a final verification step instructing the model to double-check that nothing has been missed before it replies.
Lower the effort setting, so that the model spends less of its budget filtering down its own findings.
Have it surface every finding first, then apply the threshold as a separate filtering pass.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that on Claude Opus 5 a review prompt saying "only report high-severity issues" or "be conservative" may be followed literally, so the model reports less. The stated remedy is to ask it to report everything and filter in a separate pass, which decomposes generation from filtering.

rationales.A: Strengthening the same restrictive instruction makes the literal suppression worse rather than better.
rationales.B: Claude Opus 5 verifies its own work without being told to, and explicit verification instructions cause over-verification with no quality gain; the documented advice is to remove them.
rationales.C: Anthropic notes that Claude Opus 5's review accuracy holds at lower effort settings, so lowering effort would not recover findings that a restrictive instruction had suppressed.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: A supply chain coordinator asks Claude to run a supplier onboarding checklist. The work comes back in a different order each time and one check is occasionally skipped. What should she change about the prompt?

options.text: Provide the instructions as a numbered list of sequential steps, since the order and completeness of the steps matter here.
Describe the whole task in one flowing paragraph, so that Claude is not constrained by an artificial structure imposed on it.
Repeat the most important check at the start of the prompt and again at the end, so that it cannot be overlooked.
Ask Claude to plan the work itself first and then follow whatever order of checks it decides on.

items.explanation: Under "Be clear and direct", Anthropic instructs you to provide instructions as sequential steps using numbered lists or bullet points when the order or completeness of steps matters. That is exactly the failure here: a variable order and an intermittently missing step.

rationales.B: Flowing prose is an output-format preference for the response. It is the opposite of the documented remedy when the order and completeness of the steps matter.
rationales.C: Repetition adds emphasis but not structure, and it still leaves the order of the remaining checks unstated.
rationales.D: Leaving the ordering to Claude is what is producing the variation. The documented lever is to state the sequence when the order matters.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: Anthropic's prompt engineering overview names three things you should have in place before you begin engineering a prompt. Which THREE are they? (Select THREE.)

options.text: A minimum of five worked examples of the desired output.
A clear definition of the success criteria for your use case.
A chosen model that already meets your latency and cost targets.
Some way to empirically test performance against those criteria.
A record of every prompt version you have tried so far.
A first draft prompt that you want to improve.

items.explanation: The prompt engineering overview lists exactly three prerequisites: a clear definition of the success criteria for your use case, some ways to empirically test against those criteria, and a first draft prompt you want to improve. The same page warns that not every success criterion or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering, giving latency and cost as things sometimes improved more easily by selecting a different model.

rationales.A: Examples are a technique, not a prerequisite, and the documented count is 3-5 rather than a minimum of five.
rationales.C: The page mentions model selection only as an alternative to prompt engineering for latency and cost. It is not one of the three listed prerequisites.
rationales.E: Version history is sensible practice but is not listed. The overview names exactly three prerequisites.

sources.title: Prompt engineering overview - Claude Platform Docs

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A finance business partner pastes Claude's explanation of a pricing formula into a plain-text internal wiki and finds it full of backslash and dollar-sign notation the wiki does not render. She will be running this request every week. What is the durable fix?

options.text: Ask Claude to strip the notation out afterwards in a follow-up message, and repeat that clean-up step on each weekly run.
Switch to a model that does not support mathematical notation, so that the symbols cannot be produced at all.
Add an instruction telling Claude to format the response in plain text only, with no LaTeX or markup notation.
Wrap the formula in XML tags, so that the wiki can strip the notation out automatically when it imports the text.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that Claude's latest models default to LaTeX for mathematical expressions, equations and technical explanations, and that if you prefer plain text you should add an instruction to the prompt: format the response in plain text only, using no LaTeX, MathJax or markup notation, and writing math with standard text characters. Changing the prompt fixes every future run rather than one output.

rationales.A: Post-hoc clean-up treats each output individually and has to be repeated every week. The documented fix changes the prompt so every response comes back in the required form.
rationales.B: Model choice is not the documented lever. LaTeX is a formatting default across current models and is changed by instruction.
rationales.D: XML tags separate content types inside the prompt. They do not change the notation Claude chooses inside its response.

sources.title: Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A grants administrator at a university has a Claude Opus 5 prompt template that ends with "Always double-check your answer and include a final verification step for any non-trivial task." Runs are slow and verbose, but the substantive quality is no better than before the line was added. What should he do with those instructions?

options.text: Keep them, and add a subagent whose sole job is to verify the primary answer before it is returned to the user.
Remove the verification instructions, because they cause over-verification on Opus 5 without a quality gain.
Keep them but raise the effort setting to max, so that the verification completes more quickly on each run.
Keep them and add "if in doubt, verify again", so that the check becomes unconditional on every single run.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that Claude Opus 5 verifies its own work without being told to, and that explicit verification instructions such as "include a final verification step for any non-trivial task" or "use a subagent to verify" cause over-verification. Removing them reduces wasted tokens with no loss in quality.

rationales.A: "Use a subagent to verify" is named in the same list of instructions to remove, so this compounds the problem, and the Opus 5 guidance separately says not to use subagents to double-check the model's own work.
rationales.C: Raising effort increases thinking volume. It does not remove the redundant verification behaviour and will make runs slower still.
rationales.D: Phrasing of the "if in doubt" form is separately documented as over-prompting that now causes overtriggering.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A duty manager at a city council contact centre finds Claude Opus 5's replies far too long for a channel that allows about 120 words. A colleague suggests lowering the effort setting to shorten them. What should the manager do instead, and why?

options.text: Lower the effort setting as the colleague suggests, because effort is the documented control for the length of the visible response.
Turn extended thinking off in the Claude apps, on the basis that switching thinking off reliably truncates the visible reply.
Ask Claude to re-send each reply trimmed to 120 words, because a second pass reliably enforces the word budget.
State the length requirement explicitly in the prompt, because effort controls how much the model thinks, not how much it says.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that Claude Opus 5's default user-facing responses run longer than prior Opus models', that the effort parameter controls how much the model thinks rather than how much it says, and that lowering effort can reduce thinking volume without reliably shortening the visible response. To control response length, prompt for it explicitly; a short conciseness instruction is effective.

rationales.A: This is the named trap. Effort governs thinking volume, not visible output length.
rationales.B: The help centre states that extended thinking cannot be turned off in Claude when using Claude Opus 5, and disabling thinking is not a length control in any case.
rationales.C: A trimming round trip doubles the work on every message. The documented instruction is to prompt for the length you want in the first place.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A payroll supervisor has Claude run a multi-step reconciliation that uses tools. The result is correct, but Claude moves straight from one tool call to the next and she cannot tell what it actually did without opening every result. Which prompt change addresses this?

options.text: Add an instruction asking Claude to give a quick summary of the work it has done after completing a task that involves tool use.
Ask Claude to run the tools strictly one at a time, so that each result appears separately in the transcript for her to review.
Add "if in doubt, use the tool" to the prompt, so that every instance of tool use becomes more visible.
Reduce the number of tools available to Claude, so that there is less activity for her to have to account for.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that current models are less verbose and may skip verbal summaries after tool calls, jumping directly to the next action. The stated remedy when you prefer more visibility is the sample instruction "After completing a task that involves tool use, provide a quick summary of the work you've done." This is a specific output gap fixed by a specific added instruction.

rationales.B: Serialising tool calls is documented as a way to reduce parallel execution for stability, not as a way to get visibility into what was done, and it makes the run slower.
rationales.C: "If in doubt" phrasing is documented as over-prompting that causes overtriggering. It produces more tool calls, not clearer reporting.
rationales.D: Removing capability does not create the summary she wants; the documented lever is an explicit instruction about what to report.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A management accountant's variance-commentary prompt produces commentary that is accurate but omits the year-on-year comparison the board expects, and buries the headline in the third paragraph. Which TWO iteration steps best reflect a diagnose-then-fix approach? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Reissue the same prompt with the added note "please make this better for the board."
Move the variance data below the question in the prompt so Claude reads the instruction first.
Add an explicit instruction that the commentary must include a year-on-year comparison for each variance.
Re-prompt for a more formal tone so the commentary sounds board-appropriate.
Specify positively that the response should open with the single most material variance.
Replace the prompt with a numbered list of every technique in the documentation.

items.explanation: Effective iteration means naming the specific gap and changing a specific instruction, then reissuing. The two identified gaps are a missing year-on-year comparison and a buried headline, and the two fixes state positively what the output must contain and how it must open, which is the leading documented output-control lever.

rationales.A: Vague feedback such as "make it better" names no gap and gives Claude nothing new to act on.
rationales.B: For large data-rich inputs the documented ordering is the opposite, long data at the top and the query at the end, and in any case ordering adds neither the missing comparison nor the headline.
rationales.D: Tone is not the defect. Re-toning addresses neither the missing comparison nor the ordering problem.
rationales.F: Bundling many unrelated changes into one revision makes it impossible to tell which change fixed which gap, and each of the two defects here has a specific instruction that addresses it.

sources.title: Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: Claude Opus 5 sometimes widens a narrow task, adding steps that were not requested. Which prompt change addresses that behaviour without also disrupting the self-correction the model already performs?

options.text: Add an instruction to double-check the answer before responding, so that any steps added beyond the request are caught on review.
Constrain scope explicitly: deliver what was asked at the scope intended, and flag a better approach in a sentence rather than quietly transforming the task.
Instruct the model to delegate the work to a subagent, so that a second agent decides which steps fall inside the task.
Lower the effort setting until the extra steps stop appearing, on the basis that effort determines how much work the model actually performs.

items.explanation: Two documented facts about Claude Opus 5 have to be combined. First, the model can expand the scope of a task, adding steps that were not requested, and the documented remedy for narrow tasks is to constrain scope explicitly: deliver what was asked at the scope intended, and if the request seems mistaken or a better approach exists, say so in a sentence and continue with the task as asked rather than quietly narrowing, widening or transforming it. Second, the model catches and fixes its own mistakes well without prompting, so instructions to re-check compound with behaviour it already performs.

rationales.A: Claude Opus 5 catches and fixes its own mistakes without being asked, and instructions such as "double-check your answer" compound with that behaviour, adding cost without improving results.
rationales.C: Delegation is documented as paying off on genuinely independent, sizeable tracks of work, and as multiplying cost and time on small ones; handing scope policing to a subagent leaves the request itself unbounded.
rationales.D: Effort controls how much the model thinks rather than what it decides the task is, so lowering it trades away reasoning quality while the scope of the request stays unstated.

items.stem: Anthropic's help centre distinguishes web search, extended thinking and Research largely by tool-call volume. Which pairing is correct?

Research is the right choice for looking up a single company's headquarters city.
Web search suits straightforward factual queries that need only one or two tool calls.
Research and extended thinking cannot be used together in the same request.

Extended thinking is for complex reasoning that does not require recent information, and Research is for comprehensive information gathering requiring five or more tool calls over one to three minutes.

rationales.A: Extended thinking is documented for reasoning that does not require recent information, so it must be paired with a search-based mode when freshness matters.
rationales.B: A single-fact lookup is a web-search task. Research is defined by five or more tool calls producing a multi-source synthesis.
rationales.D: The article states that Research and extended thinking can be combined, so Claude both plans its approach thoughtfully and gathers comprehensively.

items.stem: A policy researcher is setting up a complex research task in which Claude will work through a large corpus, and she needs to be able to see afterwards how the conclusions were reached. Which approach should she take?

options.text: Ask for a single best answer with no working shown, so as to keep the final output short and readable.
Define clear success criteria, ask Claude to verify across multiple sources, and have it keep research notes.
Ask Claude to settle on the first authoritative-looking source it finds, so as to keep the task short.
Supply the corpus with no instructions at all, on the basis that current models research best when left unconstrained.

items.explanation: For optimal research results Anthropic documents three things: provide clear success criteria defining what a successful answer looks like; encourage source verification by asking Claude to verify information across multiple sources; and for complex research tasks use a structured approach. rationales.A: Suppressing the working removes the transparency she needs and contradicts the documented advice to persist research notes for exactly that purpose.
rationales.C: Settling on the first source is the direct opposite of the documented instruction to verify information across multiple sources.

items.stem: An internal communications specialist wants Claude's drafts to match a plain, heading-free house voice. Which TWO adjustments are documented levers for shaping drafting output? (Select TWO.)

List every formatting element that the draft must never be allowed to contain.

Write her own prompt in the same plain style she wants back, without markdown.
Ask Claude to produce each draft twice and then pick whichever of the two reads more plainly.
Supply examples of house styles she dislikes, each one labelled as a style to avoid.

rationales.B: Prohibition lists are the documented weaker lever. Telling Claude what to do outranks telling it what not to do.

rationales.E: Producing two drafts and choosing between them is unguided resampling. It gives Claude no definition of what plain means and no documented lever is being applied.
rationales.F: Negative examples are the weaker form. Anthropic's documented preference is positive examples of the style you want.

items.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
items.stem: A quality lead asks Claude to summarise an internal standard operating procedure. Claude returns a confident summary that attributes a specific escalation threshold to "page 12 of the SOP". The lead intends to circulate the summary to shift supervisors this afternoon. What should the lead do FIRST?

options.text: Forward the summary to the SOP owner for information without reading the cited page first.
Run the same question past Claude a second time and circulate the summary if the two answers agree with each other.
Open page 12 of the SOP and confirm that it states the escalation threshold the summary claims.
Add a caveat line noting that the summary was drafted with AI assistance before circulating it.

items.explanation: A specific-looking citation is the classic surface of a fabricated detail, so the only step that addresses correctness is opening the cited page and reading it. Verification against the source is the documented first move, and it is the action the exam guide's own Domain 2 sample question keys.

rationales.A: Passing the summary on without reading the cited page moves the unverified claim closer to the people who will act on it rather than testing it.
rationales.B: A second Claude response is not independent evidence. Agreement between two model outputs is weaker than one look at the SOP, and disagreement would only tell her something is unstable.
rationales.D: Disclosure is good practice but does not establish whether page 12 says what the summary claims; supervisors would still act on a possibly fabricated threshold.

items.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
items.stem: Which of the following BEST describes how a hallucination typically presents in a Claude-generated business document?

options.text: A vague, hedged answer that avoids committing to any particular fact.
A response containing obvious spelling and grammar errors, which a reader would notice on a first pass and correct.
A refusal to answer, accompanied by an explanation of the relevant usage policy and an alternative.
A fabricated detail that looks specific and plausible, such as an invented citation or subsection number.

items.explanation: The failure is operational rather than stylistic: a language model can fabricate specific-looking details such as citation numbers. The danger is precisely that the fabrication is specific and plausible, which is why it survives a casual read and gets forwarded as fact.

rationales.A: Hedging is the opposite surface. A vague answer is easy to spot and rarely gets forwarded as fact; the concern is confident specificity.
rationales.B: Surface errors are a proofreading issue. Hallucinated content is usually fluent and well formed, which is what makes it dangerous.
rationales.C: A refusal is a safety or capability behaviour, not a fabrication of content.

items.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
items.stem: Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations lists three BASIC strategies. Which THREE of the following are those strategies? Select THREE.

options.text: Ask Claude to produce a longer answer so more supporting detail is included.
Have Claude re-read each claim after drafting and remove any claim it cannot support with a quote.
Instruct Claude to answer only in complete, formally worded sentences.
Give Claude explicit permission to say "I don't know" when it is unsure.
Ask Claude to attach a numeric confidence score to every factual claim it makes.
Ask Claude to ground its answer in direct quotes drawn from the supplied source material.

items.explanation: The three basic strategies are documented in order: allow Claude to say "I don't know", use direct quotes for factual grounding, and verify with citations by having Claude find a supporting quote for each claim after it generates a response, retracting any claim it cannot support.

rationales.A: Length is unrelated to grounding. A longer answer creates more surface area for unsupported claims, not less.
rationales.C: Formality of wording is a style control, not a hallucination control. It changes how the answer reads, not whether it is true.
rationales.E: A self-reported confidence score is not one of the documented strategies, and self-reported confidence is rejected elsewhere in the exam material as an accuracy signal.

items.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
items.stem: A knowledge manager supplies Claude with a 60-page vendor contract, well over 20,000 tokens, and asks a series of questions about the liability clauses. Which documented technique is specifically prescribed for source documents of this size to keep the answers grounded?

options.text: Split the contract across twenty separate conversations so no single context is overloaded.
Have Claude extract word-for-word quotes from the contract first, then answer using only those quotes.
Have Claude answer from general knowledge of standard commercial contracts and consult the document only if an answer looks wrong.
Have Claude condense the contract into one paragraph and answer all of the questions from that condensed version.

items.explanation: Anthropic prescribes direct-quote grounding for tasks involving long documents over roughly 20,000 tokens: ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes first, then perform the task using only those quotes. The quotes become the checkable evidence trail for every claim.

rationales.A: Fragmenting the document across conversations destroys cross-clause context and is not a documented grounding technique.
rationales.C: This is the inverse of the documented rule: no claim about a source should be made before the source has actually been read.
rationales.D: Summarising first discards the exact wording that liability analysis depends on and moves the answer one step further from the source, increasing rather than reducing fabrication risk.

items.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
items.stem: A market analyst suspects that a market-size figure in a Claude-generated briefing may be invented. The underlying source is not available to her right now. Which documented technique gives her the strongest SIGNAL that the figure may be a hallucination?

options.text: Ask Claude directly whether it is confident that the figure is accurate.
Run the same prompt several more times and check whether the figure stays consistent.
Ask Claude to rewrite the briefing in a more cautious, hedged tone.
Ask Claude to add a standing disclaimer to the briefing saying that all figures should be independently checked before use.

items.explanation: Best-of-N verification is documented as an advanced technique: run Claude through the same prompt multiple times and compare the outputs, because inconsistencies across outputs could indicate hallucinations. A grounded fact tends to reproduce; a fabricated one tends to drift.

rationales.A: Self-reported confidence is rejected as an accuracy signal, so a confident answer here would be misleading rather than informative.
rationales.C: Hedged wording changes tone only. The figure is either supported or it is not, and rewriting does not test that.
rationales.D: A blanket disclaimer transfers risk to the reader without generating any evidence about this particular figure.

items.objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
items.stem: A team has applied quote grounding, external knowledge restriction and chain-of-thought verification to a Claude workflow that drafts patient-facing medication guidance. The team lead argues that with three techniques stacked, the clinical validation step can now be removed. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Once three or more of the documented techniques are combined, the output can be treated as verified and released without further review.
Validation can be dropped provided every prompt and response is logged for later audit.
Validation is only required when Claude declines to answer or explicitly flags uncertainty.
These techniques reduce hallucinations but never eliminate them, so critical information must always be validated.

items.explanation: Anthropic states in writing that while these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations, they do not eliminate them entirely, and that critical information must always be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions. Patient-facing medication guidance is a textbook high-stakes case.

rationales.A: No documented count or combination of prompting techniques is described as removing the need for validation, so the stacking argument has no basis in the guidance.
rationales.B: Logging supports after-the-fact investigation. It does nothing to prevent an incorrect instruction reaching a patient.
rationales.C: Review is driven by the risk class of the output, not by whether the model volunteered a caveat. Relying on the model to raise its hand is the documented trap.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: An operations lead asks Claude to identify the common root causes across three long incident reports. The answer names two root causes, both of which check out, but omits a third that is stated plainly in the second report. What does this MOST directly indicate, and what should she do about it?

options.text: The answer is inaccurate, so she should discard it and treat the two named root causes as unreliable.
The answer is accurate but incomplete, so she should check the output against each report section by section.
The answer is sound, because naming two verified root causes shows the method is working.
The omission is a formatting problem, so she should ask for the findings as a table.

items.explanation: Accuracy and completeness are separate properties of an output. Every statement present can be true while material content is missing, and an omission is not detected by checking the statements that are there. The remedy is a coverage check of the output against the source, not a re-read of what was returned.

rationales.A: Nothing stated is wrong, so calling the output inaccurate misdiagnoses the defect and throws away two findings that survived checking.
rationales.C: Two correct findings say nothing about how many findings were missed. Judging completeness from the accuracy of what is present is the trap.
rationales.D: Presentation format has no bearing on whether content was omitted; the same gap would appear in a table.

items.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
items.stem: A product team asks Claude to condense several hundred pieces of customer feedback into themes for a board pack. Every theme it names checks out against the feedback, but the team wants to know whether one group of customers has been over-represented in the write-up. Which check addresses that question?

options.text: Ask Claude to state how confident it is in each theme, and treat a high rating as evidence that the themes are representative.
Count the words devoted to each theme and confirm that no theme is described at greater length than any of the others.
Compare the share of the feedback each customer group contributed with the share of the summary their concerns occupy.
Ask Claude to rewrite the summary in a more neutral tone so that no group of customers appears to be favoured.

items.explanation: Skew is a property of proportion and emphasis, not of any single statement being false, so it survives a check that only asks whether each named theme is true. The observable test is to set what went in against what came out: if a group supplied a tenth of the feedback and occupies half of the write-up, the summary is unbalanced even though nothing in it is inaccurate. Accuracy and even-handedness are separate properties and have to be checked separately.

rationales.A: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal, and it says nothing at all about which voices the summary amplified or dropped.
rationales.B: Equal word counts are a surface proxy. Themes genuinely differ in weight, and equalising their length can itself distort the picture the board receives.
rationales.D: Neutral tone changes the register of the prose. The imbalance is in what was selected and how much space it was given, which a tone rewrite leaves untouched.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: A set of test cases has been assembled to check the quality of a prompt before it is rolled out to a team. Which characteristic of that set is the clearest weakness?

options.text: The cases are graded by an automated string match rather than read and scored by a person one at a time.
The set holds more cases than any single reviewer could realistically read through in one sitting.
The cases were drawn from the team's own live workload rather than from a published benchmark set.
The cases are all clean, typical inputs, with nothing ambiguous, irrelevant or overlong among them.

items.explanation: Test cases are supposed to mirror the real task distribution, edge cases included, and the documented edge cases are irrelevant or nonexistent input data, overly long input, poor or harmful user input, and ambiguous cases where even people would struggle to agree. A set made only of clean typical inputs measures the easy half of the workload and passes a prompt that will fail the moment real material arrives. The other three characteristics are documented preferences, not defects.

rationales.A: Automated grading is the documented preference rather than a defect: more questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading beats fewer questions hand-graded by a person.
rationales.B: Volume is a documented strength of a test set, and it stops being a burden once grading is automated rather than read case by case.
rationales.C: Drawing cases from the team's own workload is what makes an evaluation task-specific; a published benchmark would be less representative of this task, not more.

items.stem: A proposal manager wants Claude to improve its own first draft in a way the bid team can inspect at each stage. Which sequence matches Anthropic's documented self-correction chaining pattern?

options.text: Generate a draft, have Claude review it against explicit criteria, then have Claude refine it.
Generate a draft, then ask Claude to confirm whether it is satisfied with what it produced.
Generate several drafts at once and have Claude pick a favourite without explaining the choice.
Generate the draft and the final polished version together in a single response so that nothing can be lost between the separate steps.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents self-correction chaining as three ordered steps: draft, review against explicit criteria, then refine based on the review. Each step is a separate call specifically so the intermediate output can be inspected, logged, evaluated or branched on.

rationales.B: A yes-or-no self-satisfaction check is a self-report, not an evaluation against explicit criteria, and carries the same weakness as self-reported confidence.
rationales.C: An unexplained preference is not a review against criteria and produces nothing a reviewer can audit or argue with.
rationales.D: Collapsing the chain into one response hides the review step, which is the part the bid team needs to see and challenge.

items.stem: A communications lead keeps receiving bulleted markdown when she wants flowing prose for a newsletter. Following Anthropic's documented order of levers for steering output format, which adjustment should she try FIRST?

XML format indicators, matching the prompt style to the desired output, and detailed formatting prompts come afterwards.

rationales.A: Matching the prompt style to the desired output is the third documented lever, not the first, and it is a heavier change than restating the instruction positively.
rationales.B: Detailed prompts for specific formatting preferences are the fourth and last documented lever, and are heavier than the situation needs.
rationales.C: Prohibition-only phrasing is the documented weaker form of the same instruction; it is listed as the thing to move away from, not the first lever.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: Before evaluating a Claude summarisation workflow, a team writes down the success criterion "the summaries should be good quality". Which of Anthropic's four documented properties of a good success criterion is this criterion MOST clearly missing?

options.text: Relevant: restate it so that it describes the model's general capability rather than this task.
Achievable: restate it as a requirement that every summary be rated perfect by every reviewer.
Measurable: restate it as a target such as an average rubric score of at least 4 out of 5.
Specific: restate it so that it names the file format each summary will be delivered in and where it will be stored.

items.explanation: Anthropic's four properties are Specific, Measurable, Achievable and Relevant. "Good quality" cannot be scored, so nothing can be compared before and after a change. The documented fix is a quantitative target, for example a rubric score threshold; the criterion is also loosely specific, but measurability is the property that stops the evaluation working at all.

rationales.A: Relevant means the criterion matters for this use case. Restating it to describe general model capability makes it less relevant, not more.
rationales.B: Achievable means basing targets on benchmarks, prior results or expert knowledge. Demanding a perfect rating from every reviewer moves away from achievable, not towards it.
rationales.D: Specificity here concerns what the summary must contain and how it will be judged, not the file format or storage location.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: Which THREE of the following appear in Anthropic's list of common success criteria for evaluating model output? Select THREE.

options.text: Task fidelity
Context utilization
Token entropy
Prompt novelty

Refusal rate

items.explanation: Anthropic enumerates eight common success criteria: task fidelity, consistency, relevance and coherence, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency and price. rationales.C: Token entropy is a sampling statistic, not one of the documented evaluation criteria.
rationales.D: Prompt novelty describes the input, not a quality of the output being evaluated, and is not on the list.

items.stem: A colleague proposes judging a new Claude summarisation workflow on five hand-picked example documents that he will read and grade himself. What is the MAIN weakness of that proposal as a way of judging the workflow?

options.text: Five hand-graded cases is too small a sample; the guidance favours many more cases graded automatically.
Hand grading is unacceptable here, because a model is better placed than a person to grade another model's output.
The proposal is sound, because careful human grading of a few worked examples is the strongest available signal of quality.
The examples should have been written by Claude rather than picked from the team's own documents.

items.explanation: Anthropic's evaluation principles are be task-specific, automate when possible, and prioritize volume over quality, stating explicitly that more questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading beats fewer questions with high-quality human hand-grading. rationales.B: Human grading is one of the documented grading families and is not ruled out; the documented principle concerns sample size and automation, not who does the grading.
rationales.C: This is the named trap. It sounds rigorous, but the documented principle deliberately favours the larger automated set over a small hand-graded one.
rationales.D: Test cases should reflect real-world use. Model-written examples would make the evaluation less task-specific, not more.

The reviewer can be confident the cited sentence supports the claim without opening the source.
The source document no longer needs to be retained anywhere, because the citation itself preserves the evidence.
Longer source documents become cheaper to process, because only the cited sentences are read.

items.stem: A finance analyst reads a Claude-drafted quarterly review. The narrative says renewals grew by a fifth, while the summary table on the following page shows renewals falling. Both figures are drawn from the same supplied data pack. What has she found, and what follows from it?

options.text: A layout fault in the table, which will resolve itself once the review is regenerated with a different table format.
An accuracy failure in the narrative specifically, so the narrative can be corrected and the table left alone as it stands.
A completeness gap, since the review needs an extra paragraph reconciling the two renewal figures for the reader.
An internal inconsistency, so both figures are in doubt and each has to be checked against the data pack.

items.explanation: Two statements in the same output contradict each other, so at most one of them can be right and neither has been established. An inconsistency tells you the pair is unsound without telling you which half is wrong, which is why the resolution is to take both figures back to the data pack rather than to pick one. Inconsistency across repeated runs is the documented Best-of-N signal, and the same reasoning applies to a contradiction inside a single response.

rationales.C: Adding a reconciling paragraph papers over the contradiction. The defect is that two stated figures disagree, not that a section is missing.

It is acceptable, because a summary is expected to omit material and accuracy is what matters here.
It is a formatting problem, and asking for a longer summary will resolve it without further checks.

items.explanation: Outputs are evaluated for accuracy and completeness, and the two properties fail independently. Here nothing stated is wrong, so the defect is coverage: a material section is missing. Naming it correctly matters, because the remedy is a coverage check of the summary against the source rather than a re-check of the statements already present.

rationales.B: Calling a true statement inaccurate misdiagnoses the defect. The summary is misleading by omission, which is a completeness failure, not an accuracy one.
rationales.C: Summaries omit detail, but a section material to the readers is not detail. Accepting the gap on accuracy grounds is the trap.
rationales.D: Length is not the issue. A longer summary produced without a coverage check can miss exactly the same section.

Short conversational answers stay inline, which is where the one-line price answer belongs.

items.stem: An HR partner uses Claude to draft candidate summaries from interview notes. Which check most directly addresses bias in those summaries, as opposed to accuracy?

Check whether the summaries apply consistent language and evaluative criteria across all candidates.
Check that each summary runs to roughly the same length, so that no one candidate receives more coverage than another.

items.explanation: Accuracy asks whether each statement is true; bias asks whether comparable cases are described in comparable terms. Consistency of language and evaluative criteria across candidates is the check that speaks to bias, and differential wording across otherwise comparable candidates is the observable signal a practitioner can act on.

rationales.C: Equal length is a superficial proxy. Two summaries of identical length can still describe comparable candidates in systematically different terms.
rationales.D: Archiving format is a records management concern and is unrelated to whether the content is even-handed.

rationales.B: A machine-readable format guarantees shape, not correctness, so it has no bearing on whether a human needs to look at the content.

items.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
items.stem: An analytics lead proposes cutting spend by moving every workflow, including a difficult multi-step data reconciliation, to the lowest-priced model available. Which line of reasoning is the strongest objection?

options.text: Batch processing discounts are by far the single largest cost lever, so the choice of model can safely be deferred
Per-token price is not the same as cost per completed task; a more capable model can cost less per task
Route every request through the cheapest available model and escalate only when a user complains about quality
Standardise on one mid-tier model at maximum effort, so that no per-model evaluation work is needed anywhere

items.explanation: Price lists are written per token, but you pay for completed tasks, so models should be compared on cost per completed task. A more capable model finishes a task with fewer turns, less searching and less backtracking, and the per-token premium is routinely overwhelmed by doing less of everything. On the DeepResearch Bench II measurements the frontier model at low effort was both more accurate and about 10 percent cheaper per task than the mid-tier model. The published advice is also to price the hardest tenth of tasks rather than the median, because a failed task bills its tokens, then the retry, then the downstream cost of the failure.

rationales.A: Prompt caching, not batch processing, was measured as the largest lever by a wide margin. Batch processing is a 50 percent discount for work that can wait up to 24 hours, and it does not change which model completes a task efficiently.
rationales.C: User complaints are not an evaluation method. The documented sequence is to build benchmark tests for the use case, test with real prompts and data, and compare on accuracy, quality and edge cases before weighing cost.
rationales.D: Maximum effort works against the finding that lower effort often matches accuracy at a fraction of the cost, and skipping evaluation removes the only reliable way to tell whether one model suits every workload.

Start with Claude Haiku 4.5, test thoroughly, evaluate, and upgrade only if a specific capability gap appears

items.explanation: The efficiency-first option is to begin implementation with Claude Haiku 4.5, test the use case thoroughly, evaluate whether performance meets requirements, and upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps. It is described as best for initial prototyping, applications with tight latency requirements, cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume straightforward tasks, which is exactly this profile.

rationales.A: This is the capability-first option, which is aimed at complex reasoning, scientific or mathematical applications, and cases where accuracy outweighs cost. It does not fit simple high-volume classification under latency pressure.
rationales.B: Fable 5 is the highest-capability and slowest tier, which conflicts with both the latency and the cost constraint; it is aimed at long-running agents and advanced research.
rationales.C: Random rotation is not a documented strategy, and it undermines evaluation because results would no longer be attributable to a specific model.

items.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
items.stem: A programme manager is deciding whether to move a working Sonnet-based workflow up to Opus. Following Anthropic's documented sequence for deciding whether to change models, what should the team do FIRST?

options.text: Move the whole workflow to the higher tier and watch for a drop in the number of user complaints
Run a handful of prompts side by side in chat and pick whichever set of answers reads better on the day
Create benchmark tests specific to the use case, which the docs call the most important step
Compare the published per-token prices of the two models and simply choose the cheaper of them

items.explanation: The documented order is: create benchmark tests specific to your use case, test with your actual prompts and data, compare performance across models on accuracy, response quality and handling of edge cases, then weigh performance and cost tradeoffs. Building the evaluation set comes first, and the docs state that having a good evaluation set is the most important step in the process.

rationales.A: Rolling out first and monitoring complaints substitutes production users for an evaluation set and gives no controlled comparison at all.
rationales.B: Informal side-by-side impressions come before any structured comparison and cannot cover edge cases; step two is testing with actual prompts and data.
rationales.D: Weighing performance against cost is the final step rather than the first, and per-token price alone is a poor proxy for cost per completed task.

items.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
items.stem: A client-facing analyst runs a report-drafting workflow on Claude Opus 5. Output quality is exactly right, but responses are slightly slower and more expensive than the team would like. What is the MOST appropriate first move?

options.text: Lower the effort level on the current model before considering a change of model
Switch straight to Claude Haiku 4.5, on the basis that it is the fastest and cheapest current model
Turn on fast mode, which raises output speed while also reducing the per-token cost of each response
Move up to Claude Fable 5, since a more capable model will finish the same work in fewer, shorter responses

items.explanation: The model-choice criteria are capabilities, speed, cost and effort, and the effort entry states that recent Opus and Sonnet models trade intelligence for latency and cost within a single model, so tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. With quality already correct, adjusting effort preserves it while addressing both speed and cost.

rationales.B: Dropping two tiers puts at risk the quality that is currently correct, and the effort lever should be tried before a model switch is considered.
rationales.C: Fast mode is a research preview on Claude Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 that delivers up to 2.5 times higher output speed at premium pricing, so it raises cost rather than reducing it.
rationales.D: Fable 5 has slower comparative latency and is priced at $10 input and $50 output per million tokens, so it worsens both of the constraints in play.

items.stem: A risk partner is scoping a project that would use Claude Fable 5 on commercially sensitive client material, and that also needs awareness of events from the past few months. Select TWO considerations she should raise.

options.text: Claude Fable 5 becomes eligible for zero data retention when it is used inside a Project
Claude Fable 5's safety classifiers can be switched off by an organisation administrator for approved internal projects
Claude Fable 5 has the latest knowledge cutoff of the current models, at May 2026, so no retrieval is needed
Claude Fable 5 carries 30-day data retention and is not available under zero data retention
Claude Fable 5's context window is capped at 200K tokens, so long client files have to be split before upload
Claude Fable 5's reliable knowledge cutoff is January 2026, so recent-events work needs web search or Research

items.explanation: Claude Fable 5 carries 30-day data retention, is not available under zero data retention, and is designated a Covered Model, which is a material constraint for sensitive workloads. Separately, reliable knowledge cutoffs differ by model: Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 are January 2026, Opus 5 is May 2026 and Haiku 4.5 is February 2025, so work on recent events should be paired with web search or Research rather than relying on model memory.

rationales.A: Nothing makes a Covered Model eligible for zero data retention through Projects. The 30-day retention designation attaches to the model itself.
rationales.B: There is no administrator setting that turns Fable 5's safety classifiers off. A declined request comes back as a normal successful response reporting the decline, and the work can be retried on a different Claude model.
rationales.C: May 2026 is Claude Opus 5's reliable knowledge cutoff, not Fable 5's. Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 are January 2026, and Haiku 4.5 is February 2025.
rationales.E: Claude Fable 5 has a 1M-token context window by default. The 200K figure belongs to Claude Haiku 4.5, the one current model without a 1M-token window.

items.stem: A 1M-token context window is documented at two levels: per model, and per claude.ai plan. Which statement is accurate on both counts?

options.text: All four current Claude models offer a 1M-token context window, and every claude.ai plan can use the full 1M tokens in one conversation
Claude Haiku 4.5 offers a 1M-token context window, while Claude Fable 5 is held at 200K tokens to keep its cost per task down
Claude Haiku 4.5 is the one current model without 1M tokens, at 200K, and on claude.ai only paid plans reach the 1M tier
Claude Fable 5, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 each need a beta header before their 1M-token window becomes available on any plan

items.explanation: Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 each have a 1M-token context window, and for every model with a 1M-token window that size is the default, with no beta header needed and standard pricing. Claude Haiku 4.5 has a 200K-token context window, making it the one current model without 1M tokens. Separately, on claude.ai the newest models support up to a 1M token context window on paid plans, while others support 500K or 200K tokens.

rationales.A: Claude Haiku 4.5 is at 200K rather than 1M, and on claude.ai the 1M tier is reached only on paid plans, with others at 500K or 200K tokens.
rationales.B: This inverts the two models. Haiku 4.5 is the 200K model, and Fable 5 has a 1M-token context window like Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.
rationales.D: For every model with a 1M-token context window, 1M is the default: no beta header is required and long-context requests are billed at standard pricing.
