items.objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
items.stem: A programme coordinator in a local authority routinely pulls documents from Google Drive into the Files section of her own projects, and the connector is working normally. When she opens a workspace that two colleagues have been added to, that upload source is greyed out. What is the reason?

options.text: The upload source is hidden once a project passes the knowledge threshold and switches into retrieval mode, because retrieval indexes only uploaded copies.
It is offered for projects that have not been shared, and it is switched off as soon as a project is shared.
Documents from that service can be added to shared projects, but only by an organization Owner or Primary Owner.
Every member of a shared project must reconnect the service before the upload source becomes visible to anyone.

items.explanation: The Google Drive connector is only available when adding to Files in private projects, and the option is disabled for shared projects. Her experience in private projects therefore does not carry over once a project is shared. Documents added through the picker in a private project sync directly from Drive, so the project keeps referencing the latest version.

rationales.A: Retrieval mode changes how knowledge is searched, not which upload sources are offered.
rationales.C: Owner status does not unlock the picker in shared projects; the restriction is not role-based.

items.objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
items.stem: A finance officer wants Claude to work from her department's budget workbook, which is an XLSX file, together with several CSV extracts drawn from it. What does she need to check before uploading them?

options.text: That the workbook has been converted to PDF beforehand, because spreadsheet data can only be read from a PDF or plain text export of the original.
That each sheet holds fewer than 20 rows, because spreadsheet uploads are truncated to the first 20 rows when they are read into a conversation.
That code execution is enabled for her account, since XLSX uploads depend on it, while CSV files are handled as ordinary documents.
That the files are added to a project rather than a chat, because spreadsheets and CSV files cannot be attached to an ordinary conversation.

items.explanation: The documented list of supported file types covers documents such as PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, HTML, ODT, RTF, EPUB and JSON, plus images and spreadsheets, and XLSX carries the additional condition that code execution must be enabled. CSV is treated as a document type and does not depend on that setting.

rationales.A: CSV and XLSX are both supported directly, so converting to PDF would discard structure for no benefit.
rationales.B: No row limit of that kind is documented; the published constraints are file size, file count and PDF page count.
rationales.D: Both file types can be attached to a chat as well as added to project knowledge, subject to the usual size and count limits.

items.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
items.stem: An executive assistant wants Claude to follow a fixed set of working rules in every conversation she has, across all of her projects and her standalone chats, without her having to select or paste anything each time. Where should the rules be configured?

options.text: In Instructions for Claude, the account-wide setting in her profile settings.
In the project instructions of each project she uses, with the same wording repeated in every one of them.
In a style that she chooses from the style menu at the start of each conversation she opens.
In a short text file uploaded to the knowledge base of each project she works in.

items.explanation: The personalization layers differ by scope: Instructions for Claude are account-wide settings that apply across all conversations, project instructions apply only to chats within that project, skills add capabilities on demand, and styles adjust tone and format. Standing rules that should never need reselecting belong in the account-wide layer.

rationales.B: This achieves the effect only inside projects, misses standalone chats, and creates duplicate copies to maintain.
rationales.C: Styles adjust tone and format of delivery and, in this scenario, would still require selection each time.
rationales.D: Knowledge files are reference material scoped to one project, not account-wide behavioural instructions.

items.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
items.stem: A business analyst uploads a custom skill for producing weekly variance commentary. It installs successfully and is enabled, but Claude never reaches for it, even on obviously relevant requests. Its one-line summary reads: Internal helper. What is the MOST appropriate fix?

options.text: Add a line to the project instructions saying CRITICAL: you MUST always use this skill for any variance work.
Re-upload the package with additional reference files bundled into the folder, so Claude has more material to draw on when the task comes up.
Install several more skills so that Claude has a broader set of capabilities to match the incoming request against.
Replace that summary with wording that states both what it does and the situations in which Claude should use it.

items.explanation: The description in a skill's frontmatter is the trigger-matching text loaded into the system prompt at startup, and it must say both what the skill does and when to use it, within a 1024-character maximum. Weak descriptions are the documented cause of trigger failures, and updating the description or instructions is the documented response to declining triggering accuracy.

rationales.A: Aggressive directive language is what recent guidance warns against, because on newer models it causes overtriggering rather than reliable triggering.
rationales.B: Bundled resources are level three content that is not read until the skill has already triggered, so they cannot improve triggering.
rationales.C: Each skill's metadata competes for attention in the system prompt, so adding more skills degrades recall rather than improving it.

items.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
items.stem: A team member tries to upload a custom skill as a ZIP file at Customize > Skills and the upload fails. Which pair of documented causes concerns the layout and contents of the package itself, rather than its file size or the characters used in its name and description?

options.text: The ZIP is larger than 30MB, or it holds more than eight files inside the skill folder.
The account has reached its skill limit, or code execution has not been used recently on the account.
The skill folder name does not match the skill name, or the required SKILL.md file is missing.
The skill was not published to the marketplace first, or it carries no version number.

items.explanation: The documented causes of a failed custom skill upload are the ZIP exceeding size limits, the skill folder name not matching the skill name, a missing required SKILL.md file, and invalid characters in the skill name or description. Of those, the folder-name mismatch and the missing SKILL.md are the packaging faults: the ZIP must contain the skill folder itself rather than loose files, and that folder must hold a SKILL.md.

rationales.A: An oversized ZIP is a documented cause, but neither 30MB nor a count of eight files is the documented threshold; 30MB is the project knowledge per-file limit, and no file-count rule is published.
rationales.B: Code execution and file creation must be enabled to use skills, but recent usage and a skill count limit are not documented upload failures.
rationales.D: Custom skills are uploaded directly and do not require marketplace publication or a version number to install.

items.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
items.stem: Anthropic describes skills as using three-level progressive disclosure to control how much context they consume. Which TWO statements about what this means in practice are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Installing many skills carries only a small standing cost, because until a skill triggers only its name and description occupy context.
The full instruction body of every installed skill is loaded at startup so that Claude can compare them before choosing one.
Bundled reference files consume context as soon as the skill is installed, whether or not Claude ever reads them.
Bundled scripts contribute only their results to the conversation, never their code.
Skills are processed outside the context window, so an installed skill has no effect at all on the context available for a conversation.
Bundled files must be deleted after each use to release the context that they occupy in the conversation.

items.explanation: Level one metadata is loaded at startup at roughly 100 tokens per skill, which is why you can install many skills without a context penalty: until a skill is triggered, only its name and description occupy context. Bundled scripts are run rather than read, so the script code itself never enters the context window and only its output consumes tokens.

rationales.B: The SKILL.md body is level two content and loads only when the skill is triggered, not at startup.
rationales.C: Level three bundled resources cost nothing until they are actually accessed.
rationales.E: Skills do occupy context, which is exactly why progressive disclosure exists; the standing cost is small rather than zero.
rationales.F: Bundled files sit on the filesystem and are read only when needed; there is no cleanup step to reclaim context.

items.stem: On a Team plan, a member follows a colleague's instructions to add a skill but cannot find the Skills area at all. Nothing has been configured for skills in the organization yet. What has to happen first?

options.text: The organization must install a plugin first, because on a Team plan skills are only ever delivered inside plugins.
An Owner must enable both Code execution and file creation and Skills in Organization settings > Skills.
The organization must upgrade to Enterprise, because skills are not offered to Team plan members.
Each member must enable Code execution and file creation in their own Settings > Capabilities.

rationales.C: Skills are available on Team; only certain governance features such as skill and plugin scanning are Enterprise.
rationales.D: Self-service enablement in a member's own settings is the Free, Pro and Max path, not the Team path.

items.stem: In the unified Customize directory, how does a plugin differ from a skill or a connector?

options.text: A plugin is a skill that an Owner has shared with the rest of the organization.
A plugin is an authenticated integration to an external service such as Gmail, Google Drive or Slack.
A plugin is a folder of instructions and resources that Claude loads only when relevant.
A plugin is a saved set of tone and formatting preferences applied to responses.
A plugin is a package that bundles skills, connectors and sub-agents into one installable item.

items.stem: A freelance researcher on a Pro plan has built a carefully configured project and wants two collaborators to read its instructions and knowledge and chat inside it, without changing anything. What should she be told?

options.text: Project sharing, including the Can view permission she wants, is available only on Team and Enterprise plans.
She can share the project on Pro by adding the two collaborators with Can view permission from the project menu.
She can share on Pro, but only with Can edit permission, because Can view is reserved for Enterprise organizations.
Sharing is available on all plans once the project has at least one knowledge file attached to it.

items.explanation: Project sharing is documented as a Team and Enterprise capability with two permission levels, Can view, which allows access to project contents, knowledge and instructions plus chatting but no editing, and Can edit. A Pro account cannot share a project, so the collaborators would need to be in a Team or Enterprise organization.

rationales.B: Can view exists as a permission level, but the sharing feature itself is not offered on Pro.
rationales.C: Both permission levels sit with Team and Enterprise; neither is available on Pro, and Can view is not Enterprise-only.

items.objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
items.stem: A team lead on a Team plan has built a custom skill and wants to publish it to the organization's skills directory so that every colleague can find it. Members already create and use skills day to day, but no Share button appears anywhere on the skill. What has to happen first?

options.text: The skill must pass skill and plugin security scanning before a Share button is offered to the person who created it.
Each colleague must upload their own copy of the skill, after which the sharing controls become available.
An Owner must enable the sharing toggles in Organization settings > Skills, because skill sharing is off by default.
The skill must be published to the public Claude directory first, because organization sharing builds on that listing.

items.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans a member can share a skill with specific people, with a group, or with the entire organization, in which case it is published to the organization's directory. Sharing is off by default: an Owner goes to Organization settings > Skills and enables the skill sharing, share with groups or share with organization toggles, or a combination of them, before the Share button appears. Shared skills are view-only for recipients, and updates propagate to them automatically.

rationales.A: Skill and plugin security scanning is a separate Enterprise beta that blocks unsafe skills from use; it does not gate the sharing controls.
rationales.B: Recipients of a shared skill enable and use it without uploading their own copy, so extra uploads would not produce a Share button.
rationales.D: There is no requirement to publish a skill publicly before it can be shared inside an organization.

items.objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
items.stem: Which TWO statements about skill and plugin scanning on Claude Enterprise are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Scanning also covers skills that are uploaded through the Skills API or from the Claude Console.
Skills that already existed in the organization before scanning was turned on are scanned retroactively the next time they are used.
A scan returns Pass, Warn or Fail; a skill that passes with a warning stays usable behind a caution notice, and a failed skill is blocked.
Scanning replaces the manual review checklist for third-party skills, so an organization that turns it on no longer needs a separate audit step.
Scanning applies to skills uploaded or edited in claude.ai and Cowork, and a skill whose scan has not finished is also blocked.
Scanning is turned on by default for every Team and Enterprise organization as soon as skills are enabled.

items.explanation: A skill that fails the scan, or whose scan has not finished, is blocked from use, while a skill that passes with a warning stays usable behind a caution notice. Scanning covers skills that members upload or edit in claude.ai and Claude Cowork after an Owner or Primary Owner turns the beta on.

rationales.A: Skills uploaded through the Skills API, including from the Claude Console, are an explicit exclusion.
rationales.B: Skills already present when scanning was turned on are excluded, as are Claude-created and MCP-server skills.
rationales.D: Scanning complements the review checklist rather than replacing it, and it will not catch a skill that behaves unintentionally without being malicious.
rationales.F: It is a beta that an Owner or Primary Owner turns on for a Claude Enterprise organization, and organizations using customer-managed encryption keys, zero data retention or HIPAA-ready configurations are excluded.

Ask an Owner to disable memory for the whole organization.
Delete the project summary held for each of her projects.
Pause memory.

Uploading the skill once on claude.ai makes it available automatically in Claude Code project folders and in the Claude API workspace for the same organization, with nothing further to do.

After a model update the same tool now fires on requests where it is plainly irrelevant. What should he change first?

Dial back the aggressive language to normal phrasing such as Use this tool when.
Remove the tool from the shared configuration and reintroduce it only for specific conversations that need it.
Add matching emphatic wording to the other tools so that they all compete on equal terms.

The same point appears in the migration guidance for that generation, which advises tuning down anti-laziness prompting.

rationales.A: The documented ordering guidance concerns placing long documents near the top and the query at the end; it does not address emphasis-driven overtriggering.

items.stem: A retail chain uses Claude to draft the rejection letters sent to unsuccessful external job applicants. A qualified HR professional reads and signs off every letter before it goes out, but the letters say nothing about how they were produced. What still needs to change before the letters are sent?

options.text: Nothing needs to change, because a qualified professional already reviews every letter before it is sent.
A second independent reviewer must countersign each letter before it can be disseminated.
Applicants must be told that AI was used to help produce the decision they receive.
The use case must be registered with Anthropic as high risk before any letter is sent.

items.explanation: Employment and housing is one of Anthropic's named high-risk use case categories. Two requirements attach: a qualified professional must review the content or decision prior to dissemination, and where model outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers the organisation must disclose that AI was used to help produce the advice, decision or recommendation. The scenario satisfies the review requirement but not the disclosure requirement, so the gap is disclosure to the applicant.

rationales.A: Qualified review is only one of the two requirements; the disclosure duty is separate and is not met by an internal sign-off.
rationales.B: The policy calls for review by a qualified professional in the field, not for a second countersignature.
rationales.D: There is no pre-launch registration or notification step with Anthropic for high-risk use cases.

items.stem: A consultant is reviewing five proposed client deployments of Claude, all of which produce output that reaches members of the public. Which TWO require both review by a qualified professional before dissemination and disclosure to the affected individual that AI was used? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A tool that generates subject lines for a retailer's promotional email campaigns.
A tool that drafts tenancy application outcomes sent to prospective renters.
A tool that summarises publicly available product manuals into shorter customer help articles.
A tool that suggests wording for a company's public social media replies about opening hours.
A tool that produces first-draft news stories published on a client's public news site.

items.explanation: The named high-risk categories in Anthropic's Usage Policy are legal, healthcare, insurance, finance, employment and housing (treated as one combined category), academic testing, accreditation and admissions, and media or professional journalistic content. Tenancy outcomes fall in the employment and housing category and published news drafts fall in media or professional journalistic content. Each requires review by a qualified professional before dissemination and disclosure to the affected individual that AI was used.

rationales.A: Promotional marketing copy is not a named high-risk category; it remains subject to the Universal Usage Standards only.
rationales.C: Summarising public product documentation carries no elevated harm profile and is not in any named high-risk category.
rationales.D: Routine replies about opening hours are ordinary commercial use; if this became a consumer-facing chatbot, the separate chatbot disclosure guideline would apply instead.

items.objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
items.stem: A hospital's clinical coding team uses Claude entirely internally: qualified coders paste de-identified case summaries, review every output themselves, and no Claude-derived text ever reaches a patient. The compliance lead asks whether the Usage Policy's high-risk requirements are engaged. What is the MOST accurate response?

options.text: Disclosure is triggered by the healthcare category itself, regardless of whether any output ever reaches a patient.
Both high-risk requirements are scoped to outputs presented directly to individuals or consumers, so neither is triggered here.
De-identifying the inputs removes the use case from the high-risk healthcare category entirely, so no requirement can attach.
Disclosure applies immediately, while qualified professional review becomes mandatory only once identifiable patient data enters the workflow.

items.explanation: The Usage Policy scopes both high-risk requirements the same way. Qualified human review is required when the products or services are used to provide advice, recommendations or subjective decision-making directly affecting individuals or consumers, and disclosure is required if model outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers. Purely internal coding work reviewed by qualified staff engages neither requirement on its own, although the qualified review the team already performs remains the prudent control and both duties would attach the moment output is disseminated.

rationales.A: The category alone is not the test; both requirements attach only where output affects or is presented to individuals or consumers.
rationales.C: De-identification reduces privacy risk, but it is dissemination to individuals or consumers, not identifiability, that governs whether the requirements attach.
rationales.D: This invents an asymmetry the policy does not contain: both requirements share the same individual- or consumer-facing scoping.

items.stem: A marketing manager asks Claude for competitor market-share percentages, receives a confident set of figures, and is about to paste them straight into a board pack. Using Anthropic's AI Fluency framework, which of the four competencies is she about to skip?

options.text: Delegation: deciding to hand the whole market-sizing exercise to Claude rather than keeping parts of it in human hands.
Diligence: adding a line to the board pack saying Claude produced the figures, which settles the risk.
Description: rephrasing the request with far more context so that the figures come out accurate.
Discernment: critically evaluating the output and verifying the figures before a consequential decision.

items.explanation: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework sets out four competencies, the 4Ds: Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence. Discernment is the competency covering critical evaluation of outputs and keeping human judgement at consequential decision points. A board pack is exactly such a point, so the figures must be checked against a real source before they are used.

rationales.A: Delegation concerns what goes to AI and what stays human; delegating more of the task would increase the unverified content rather than address it.
rationales.B: Noting that Claude produced a number does not make the number correct; verification is still required before it informs a decision.
rationales.C: A better-specified prompt may improve relevance, but no amount of rephrasing makes unverified figures trustworthy.

A per-user Model Improvement control in Privacy Settings at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls.
Anthropic uses all consumer conversations by default, and users may request removal afterwards.
A central organisation administrator policy applied across all consumer accounts in the region.

It stays visible in chat history for 30 days and is then removed from storage.
It is kept for 5 years, because deleted conversations are preserved for later safety review.

items.stem: A recruitment team drafts job adverts with Claude. A reviewer notices that the drafts keep reaching for language associated with one demographic profile, although the role is open to everyone. The team lead argues that published model evaluations already cover bias, so the wording can be trusted. What is the sound response?

options.text: Model-level evaluations describe the model, not this deployment, so the drafts need a human check for skewed wording before publication.
The published evaluations settle the question for this deployment as well, so individual drafts need no further reading before they go out.
Asking Claude in a follow-up turn to make the wording neutral removes the skew reliably, so no human check of the final text is needed.
Adding a note that the adverts were drafted with AI assistance removes the risk, because readers can then discount the wording for themselves.

items.explanation: Published model reports describe how a model behaved on a fixed evaluation set; they characterise the model in aggregate and say nothing about the wording of a particular advert produced in a particular deployment. Critically evaluating the output before it is used is the Discernment competency in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework, and employment content that reaches candidates sits in a category the Usage Policy singles out for extra care, including disclosure to the people who receive it.

rationales.B: An aggregate result on a test set is not evidence about the drafts this team is about to publish.
rationales.C: A follow-up instruction can change the wording, but it is still unverified output; something has to read the result.
rationales.D: Disclosure and bias are separate duties, and telling readers AI was involved does not make skewed wording acceptable.

When a conversation is flagged for safety review, or she explicitly reports material to Anthropic.

Opting out is therefore not absolute, and this is the practical governance point for anyone relying on the control.

rationales.B: Consumer accounts are not governed by an organisation administrator; tenant-level controls belong to Team and Enterprise plans.

items.stem: A risk officer is signing off a Claude Cowork rollout. One team wants Cowork to work through a shared folder of documents received from external parties, with connector tools allowed to run without per-task approval. What is the strongest reason to refuse that configuration as it stands?

options.text: Cowork is unable to open documents that originated outside the organisation, so the proposed workflow would fail at the very first externally supplied file.
Connector tools remain unavailable inside Cowork until an owner signs a zero data retention agreement covering the whole workspace and everyone in it.
Cowork sessions are excluded from the Compliance API altogether, so the organisation would hold no record at all of what the team did with the files.
Cowork pairs agentic autonomy with internet access, so injected instructions in external content are a live risk and write-capable tools belong behind approval.

items.explanation: Anthropic states that Cowork carries unique risks because of its agentic nature and internet access, and that despite the safety measures in place the risk of prompt injection attacks is non-zero. The published advice is to avoid granting access to sensitive files and to watch Claude for suspicious actions. The organisation setting that lets members save an always-allow preference for connector tools is off by default, so members approve write-capable tools per task; turning that protection off for a folder of untrusted external documents removes the check at exactly the point it matters.

rationales.A: Cowork can work with externally supplied files; the problem is that their content is untrusted, not that it cannot be read.
rationales.B: Zero data retention governs what Anthropic stores and is not a precondition for using connector tools at all.
rationales.C: Cloud Cowork sessions are captured in the Compliance API, and Enterprise admins can retrieve local session content through it in beta.

items.stem: An organisation on a standard Claude for Work commercial plan learns that a user submitted content which Anthropic's automated trust and safety systems flagged as a Usage Policy violation. The security lead assumes it will be discarded on the ordinary retention cycle. What is the accurate position?

options.text: The flagged content is deleted on the ordinary cycle and only the classifier score is kept, for 2 years from the flag.
Flagged inputs and outputs may be kept for up to 2 years, and classification scores for up to 7 years.
Flagged content is retained for 5 years, matching the retention period applied to submitted feedback.
The organisation's own retention setting takes precedence, so the content is removed within 30 days.

Anthropic states that in all cases it may retain chats or sessions as required by law or as necessary to combat violations of the Usage Policy, so enforcement retention is not switched off by the organisation's ordinary retention configuration.

rationales.A: This reverses the two figures and drops the separate 7-year retention of classification scores.
rationales.C: Five years relates to de-identified data in consumer training pipelines and to feedback submissions, not to violation-flagged content.
rationales.D: Retention settings govern ordinary data; the stated exception for combating Usage Policy violations sits above them.

items.stem: Anthropic publishes political even-handedness results for its models, measured across paired requests that present opposing viewpoints on a fixed set of topics. What may a deploying organisation legitimately conclude from a strong result?

options.text: That the model engaged with both requests in each pair to a comparable standard on that test set, which is not a statement about any single output.
That outputs on contested topics are balanced in practice, so a reviewer no longer needs to read individual drafts on those topics before they are circulated.
That the organisation inherits the published result as evidence of its own compliance with a regulator's fairness expectations for automated content.
That the result carries across every model in the current Claude line-up, because the evaluation is run once for each model generation.

items.explanation: The published evaluation spans paired requests presenting opposing political viewpoints across a fixed set of topics and task types, and scores whether the model engages with both requests in a pair with comparable depth and quality, whether it acknowledges opposing viewpoints, and how often it declines to answer. rationales.B: An aggregate score on a test set says nothing about the specific draft in front of a reviewer, so the review step stays.
rationales.C: The evaluation is Anthropic's account of its own model; a deployer's regulatory position rests on its own controls.
rationales.D: Results are published per model report, and one model's score does not transfer to the others in the line-up.

Local Cowork history is retained by Anthropic for 30 days and can be exported by an owner at any point within that window.
Local Cowork history can be exported only after zero data retention is enabled for the whole organisation.

A single flat list of prohibited uses that applies identically to every customer, on every plan and in every region.
Two tiers: consumer standards and commercial standards, applied according to the customer's plan type.
Four tiers aligned to the AI Safety Levels defined in Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy.

items.explanation: The Usage Policy has three tiers: Universal Usage Standards that apply to everyone, High-Risk Use Case Requirements that apply to specific consumer-facing use cases, and Additional Use Case Guidelines covering certain other uses such as consumer-facing chatbots.

rationales.B: A flat prohibited-uses list was the older mental model; the restructured policy layers requirements by risk.

A shift of responsibility for high-risk use cases from the customer to Anthropic.
Replacement of the policy by the Responsible Scaling Policy for all commercial customers.
New disclosure obligations requiring organisations to tell their own end users that they are interacting with AI.

items.stem: An insurance firm plans to use Claude to draft claim decision explanations that are sent directly to policyholders. Which TWO measures must be in place before the first explanation is sent? (Select TWO.)

A zero data retention agreement covering the claims workload end to end.
Review by a qualified professional before the output is disseminated.
An independent third-party bias audit of the drafting model, repeated every quarter.
Disclosure to the affected policyholder that AI was used.
Storage of all drafts for seven years to support later appeals.

items.explanation: Each named high-risk category triggers two mandatory measures together: a qualified professional in that field must review the content or decision prior to dissemination or finalisation, and where model outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers the organisation must disclose that AI was used, at a minimum at the beginning of each session. Candidates commonly treat these as alternatives when in fact both are required.

rationales.A: No pre-launch registration of high-risk use cases with Anthropic is required by the policy.
rationales.B: Zero data retention is a separate, approval-gated commercial arrangement and is not a high-risk requirement.
rationales.D: A recurring third-party bias audit may be good practice, but it is not one of the two stated high-risk measures.
rationales.F: The seven-year figure relates to trust and safety classification scores for flagged content, not to a drafting retention duty.

Financial penalties scaled to account spend, with appeals heard by an external ombudsman.
Warning, suspending or terminating access, with an appeals process through which some bans are overturned.
Referral of every case to a national regulator, which then decides on account access.

rationales.B: Financial penalties and an external ombudsman are not part of Anthropic's published enforcement model.

items.stem: A support manager is launching a customer-facing chatbot built on Claude. Legal has added a line to the website terms of service stating that automated assistance may be used. Is that sufficient disclosure?

Yes, provided the chatbot also confirms it is an AI whenever a customer asks it directly.
No: the disclosure must be repeated in every individual message the chatbot sends.
No: users must be told they are interacting with AI at the beginning of each chat session.

A one-time notice buried in terms of service does not meet the requirement.

rationales.B: Answering honestly on request is good practice but does not replace proactive disclosure at the start of the session.
rationales.C: Per-message disclosure exceeds what is required; the stated minimum is at the beginning of each session.

items.stem: A communications director in Canada asks whether Claude's text watermarking affects her team, since the EU AI Act does not apply to them. What is the correct answer?

options.text: It affects them: Anthropic applies watermarking globally, because it has no durable way to scope it by region.
It does not affect them, because watermarking is applied only to sessions that originate inside the European Union.
It affects them only if their workspace owner opts in to watermarking in the organisation's settings.
It does not affect them, because watermarking is applied only to generated image and document files, not to text.

items.explanation: Anthropic states that it is applying watermarking globally at launch because it does not yet have a durable way to scope it by region, and that it will keep evaluating other approaches. The 2 August 2026 date belongs to the EU, which from that date requires providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content; Anthropic publishes no start date of its own, says future Claude models will generate watermarked text, and is working to add watermarking to models launched before that date under the law's transition period. No user opt-out is documented.

rationales.B: Region-scoped application is precisely what Anthropic says it has no durable way to do, so the measure is global.
rationales.C: No opt-in or opt-out control for watermarking is documented at user or workspace level.
rationales.D: Files receive C2PA content credentials in their metadata, but text output is separately watermarked, so text-based teams are in scope.

items.objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
items.stem: An academic integrity officer wants to use Claude's text watermark as evidence in misconduct cases. Which TWO documented limitations should temper that plan? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It survives only while the text stays inside the Claude interface and is lost on copy-paste.
The signal is weak or absent in short passages and sparse in code or terminology-bound text.
It can be switched off by the user for a given conversation.
It is embedded only in the first paragraph of a response.
It reliably separates text Claude wrote from text Claude only lightly edited.
It cannot identify an individual user, organisation or conversation.

items.explanation: The watermark works by seeding the choice among equally valid word options from a secret key plus the preceding words, producing a machine-detectable statistical pattern. Anthropic states that detection does not work well on small samples, where there are fewer word choices to go on, and that code, which often has to be exact, generally carries less watermarking than other text. It also states that nothing in the watermark or its key would let anyone recover information about the user, and that light editing probably will not remove the watermark while a complete rewrite replacing every word will.

rationales.A: The pattern lives in the word choices themselves, so it survives copy-paste; a full rewrite is what destroys it.
rationales.C: No user opt-out or per-conversation switch for watermarking is documented.
rationales.D: The signal accumulates across the whole passage rather than being confined to the opening paragraph.
rationales.E: Light editing probably will not remove the watermark, so its presence does not separate text Claude wrote from text Claude only touched up.

items.objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
items.stem: A communications team asks Claude to summarise both sides of a contested policy debate for a client briefing. The draft reads well and the briefing is due in an hour. What is the minimum responsible step before it is sent?

options.text: Send it as drafted, since balance on contested topics is exactly what the model's published evaluations are designed to guarantee for every individual response.
Ask Claude whether its own summary is balanced, and send the briefing unchanged as soon as the model confirms that it is.
Read the draft for one-sided framing and check it against the underlying sources, because model-level testing does not make any single output balanced.
Add a note to the briefing saying the summary was produced with AI, which passes the judgement about balance across to the client.

items.explanation: Anthropic's published even-handedness results measure a model in aggregate across a fixed evaluation set. They do not certify that a particular summary is balanced, so a consequential document still needs a human to read it against its sources. That critical evaluation of output is the Discernment competency in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework.

rationales.A: Aggregate evaluation results describe the model, not the individual response about to be sent to a client.
rationales.B: Asking a model to grade its own output adds no independent evidence that the summary is even-handed.
rationales.D: Disclosure tells the client how the text was made; it does not correct one-sided framing or transfer the duty to check.

Anthropic's Transparency Hub, which centralises model reports and model cards.
The Trust Portal, which is the source for model evaluation methodology.
The organisation's admin console, which surfaces per-model evaluation results for the plan's enabled models.

items.stem: Anthropic signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, published by the European Commission in July 2026, alongside around 190 other signatories. What is the relationship between the Code and the binding EU requirement?

options.text: The Code is voluntary; what binds providers is the EU requirement to mark AI-generated content, which applied from 2 August 2026.
The Code is mandatory for every provider placing an AI system on the EU market, and signing it is the way in which compliance is formally recorded.
Signing the Code replaces the underlying EU transparency obligations with the Code's own lighter, self-assessed requirements for signatories.
Signing the Code grants signatories an exemption from transparency penalties for their first two years of commercial operation in the EU.

items.explanation: Anthropic states that it signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content in July 2026 along with several other major model providers and around 190 signatories in total, and that it is implementing watermarking to comply with the EU AI Act. The Code is a voluntary instrument. The binding requirement is the EU obligation that providers serving its market mark AI-generated content, which applied as of 2 August 2026, with a transition period for models launched before that date. Signing is reported as a route to demonstrating conformity, but the obligation itself comes from the AI Act.

rationales.B: The Code is voluntary; it is the AI Act transparency obligation, not the Code, that binds providers in the EU market.
rationales.C: Following the Code is a way of meeting the underlying obligations rather than substituting a lighter regime for them.
rationales.D: No penalty holiday follows from signing, because a voluntary code cannot suspend a statutory obligation.

items.stem: A bid manager pastes a large tender document plus eight supporting attachments into a single claude.ai conversation. Claude responds with 'Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat.' She still needs to work on the tender today. What does Anthropic's documented guidance tell her to do?

options.text: Reduce the content she is sending by attaching fewer or smaller files, or start a new conversation.
Report the message at status.claude.com and wait for the incident to be marked resolved.
Wait for her 5-hour usage window to reset, then send exactly the same message again.
Move to a higher-priced plan, since the paid tiers do not apply a maximum length to any single chat.

items.explanation: Anthropic's error-message troubleshooting article attributes this string to input exceeding the maximum allowed message length, and the message itself names the documented fixes: try attaching fewer or smaller files, or start a new conversation. It is a length problem, not an availability or entitlement problem.

rationales.B: status.claude.com covers genuine service incidents. A length-limit message is a normal validation response to the user's own input and is not an incident to report.
rationales.C: This is a length-limit message, not a usage-limit message. Waiting for the 5-hour session window to reset changes nothing, because resending the same over-length input will produce the same error.
rationales.D: The maximum message and chat length is a constraint on the input being sent, and it applies on every plan. The documented remedies are attaching fewer or smaller files or starting a new conversation, not upgrading.

items.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
items.stem: A procurement analyst's long-standing prompt for comparing supplier contracts has started returning vague, drifting answers. Her manager suggests moving the team to a higher plan tier and a larger model to fix it. Following Anthropic's documented approach to an unhelpful answer, what should she do FIRST?

options.text: Move the team to the larger model at once, because answer quality tracks model size.
Work through the prompt remedies: state the ask clearly, add context, and break it into substeps.
Raise the effort setting to its maximum and leave the prompt itself exactly as it is.
Upgrade the plan tier first, since higher tiers are documented to produce more accurate answers.

items.explanation: Anthropic's help centre gives four ordered remedies for an unhelpful answer: explain your ask simply and clearly; include as much context as possible, as though instructing someone with no background knowledge; break down complex requests into substeps; and give Claude feedback through follow-ups, clarifications or a request to rewrite. The prompt is what gets examined first. Anthropic's prompt engineering overview separately notes that not every failing result is best solved by prompt engineering, but the problems it points at model selection to solve are latency and cost.

rationales.A: Model selection is the documented lever for latency and cost. Reaching for a larger model before checking clarity, context and structure skips every documented remedy for a weak answer.
rationales.C: Effort governs how much the model thinks, not whether the request is clear. Leaving an under-specified prompt untouched leaves the actual defect in place while consuming more usage.
rationales.D: Plan tier governs usage allowances and feature access, not answer accuracy. No documentation ties response quality to the price of the subscription.

items.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
items.stem: A communications lead has already replaced her prohibition with a positive instruction ('Compose your response as smoothly flowing prose paragraphs'), but Claude still returns heavily bulleted markdown. Her own brief is written as a dense bulleted list. Which documented lever should she try NEXT?

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm at the end of each draft that no markdown was used anywhere.
Add the original 'do not use markdown or bullet points' line back alongside the positive one.
Rewrite the brief itself in plain prose, since prompt style influences response style.
Lower the effort setting, because effort is the documented control for output structure.

items.explanation: Anthropic lists four format-steering levers in order. She has already applied the first (say what to do rather than what not to do). The next documented lever is matching prompt style to the desired output: the formatting style used in your prompt may influence Claude's response style, and removing markdown from your prompt can reduce the volume of markdown in the output. The remaining lever after that is detailed explicit formatting guidance.

rationales.A: Asking for self-confirmation is a verification step, not a steering step. It reports on the format after the fact and does nothing to change how the draft is produced.
rationales.B: Reinstating the prohibition reverses the lever she has already applied correctly. Telling Claude what to do outranks telling it what not to do, and stacking both back together does not add a new mechanism.
rationales.D: Effort governs how much the model thinks; it is not a formatting control and does not reliably reshape visible output structure or style.

items.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
items.stem: An office manager receives an answer that is broadly right but omits one section she needs. The fourth remedy in Anthropic's help centre article on unhelpful answers applies directly here. What is it?

options.text: Submit the missing section to Anthropic through the status page so the gap is logged.
Open a brand new conversation and send the identical prompt again until a complete answer comes back.
Raise the effort level and resend, because completeness is governed by the effort setting.
Reply in the same conversation with follow-up instructions, clarifications, or a rewrite request.

rationales.B: Resending an unchanged prompt supplies no new information, so there is no documented reason to expect a different result. The listed remedy is to give Claude feedback, not to repeat the request.
rationales.C: Effort governs how much the model thinks, not which sections it includes. A missing requirement is addressed by stating the requirement.

items.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
items.stem: An operations lead has a reusable prompt that pastes a customer email thread, a policy extract and her own instructions into one continuous block of text. Claude sometimes treats sentences from the pasted email as instructions and answers the wrong question. Which documented change addresses this?

options.text: Wrap each kind of content in its own tag, such as instructions, context and input.
Repeat her instructions word for word at the very end of the prompt as a reminder.
Ask Claude to restate the instructions it identified before it answers the question.
Put her own instructions in capital letters so they stand out from the pasted material.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents XML tags as the way to help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously, especially when a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples and variable inputs. Wrapping each type of content in its own tag, for example instructions, context and input, reduces misinterpretation. The same guidance advises consistent, descriptive tag names and nesting where the content has a natural hierarchy.

rationales.B: Repetition adds tokens without creating a boundary, and the pasted email still sits in the same undifferentiated block, so the same sentences can still be read as instructions.
rationales.C: Asking Claude to restate its understanding is a verification step. It may surface the misreading after the fact but does not prevent it, and adds over-verification overhead on every run.
rationales.D: Capitalisation is emphasis, not structure. It creates no boundary between the instruction block and the pasted material, which is what the model is misreading.

items.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
items.stem: A finance manager asks Claude to explain a variance calculation in writing. The explanation is correct, but the formulas come back in LaTeX notation that her word processor renders as raw markup. What does Anthropic document as the fix?

options.text: Lower the effort setting, which makes Claude choose simpler mathematical notation.
Instruct Claude to answer in plain text and write expressions with ordinary characters.
Switch to a smaller model, since only the larger models default to LaTeX notation.
Accept it and convert afterwards, since the notation default cannot be changed by prompting.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that Claude's latest models default to LaTeX for mathematical expressions, equations and technical explanations, and gives a prompt-level remedy for users who prefer plain text: format the response in plain text only, with no LaTeX, MathJax or markup notation, writing math expressions with standard text characters such as / for division, * for multiplication and ^ for exponents.

rationales.A: Effort governs how much the model thinks, not the notation it renders output in. It is not a formatting control.
rationales.C: The LaTeX default is documented as behaviour of Claude's latest models generally, not a property of one size tier, so changing model is not the documented control.

items.stem: Mid-morning, several staff report seeing 'Due to unexpected capacity constraints, Claude is unable to respond...' The operations lead checks status.claude.com and sees all systems operational. The team asks whether to raise a major incident with the vendor. What is the MOST appropriate response?

Assume the 5-hour session limit was reached and tell staff to wait for the window to reset.
Treat it as normal load management and have people retry in a few minutes.
Raise a major incident, since a message absent from the status page means an unreported outage.

items.stem: A training coordinator has collected examples from staff of Claude answers that were unhelpful or misleading, and wants to pass them back to Anthropic. Which route does Anthropic's help centre document for this?

items.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
items.stem: A consultant cannot sign in and sees 'There was an error logging you in'. Colleagues on the same plan are working normally at the same moment. Which sequence matches Anthropic's documented troubleshooting for this message?

options.text: Disable VPN and browser extensions, clear cache and cookies, then check the status page.
Buy a usage bundle, since sign-in fails once the weekly usage limit has been exhausted.
Reinstall the operating system, as the documented cause is a corrupted local user profile.
Wait five hours for the session window to reset, which restores access to the account.

items.explanation: Anthropic attributes this message to various technical issues during authentication and lists the remedies as disabling a VPN, deactivating browser extensions, clearing cache and cookies, and checking the status page. Colleagues working normally makes a service-wide problem unlikely, which is why the local, client-side steps come before escalation.

rationales.B: Usage limits produce their own distinct banners and restrict what Claude will process, not whether the account can authenticate. Credits do not affect sign-in.
rationales.C: This is not a documented cause or remedy, and it is disproportionate to a message whose published fixes are all lightweight browser-side steps.
rationales.D: The 5-hour session window governs usage consumption, not authentication. Waiting does not address a login failure.

items.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
items.stem: In a chat where no web search was used, Claude confidently describes a product launch that never took place. According to Anthropic's help centre, what best explains this?

options.text: Claude always states when it does not know something, so the answer is probably right.
Claude can hallucinate, and may lack up-to-date training data about current events.
Claude only produces incorrect answers when the account is close to its usage limit.
This is a service fault, and it will appear as an incident on the Claude status page.

items.explanation: Anthropic describes hallucinated information as a byproduct of some of the current limitations of frontier generative AI models, and notes that Claude might not have been trained on the most up-to-date information and may get confused when prompted about current events. The documented user-side responses are to scrutinise high-stakes advice carefully and to check original sources.

rationales.A: Claude does not reliably announce the boundary of its knowledge, and self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal. A confident tone is not evidence of correctness.
rationales.C: Nothing in the documentation links accuracy to how much of the usage limit has been consumed. Usage limits govern how much work can be done, not how correct it is.
rationales.D: An incorrect answer is a documented model limitation rather than a service incident, so it will not appear on the status page, which covers availability.

items.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
items.stem: A knowledge manager must demonstrate that a revised Claude prompt for triaging support tickets genuinely performs better than the old one. She has time to build one evaluation set. Which design best matches Anthropic's published evaluation guidance?

options.text: A set of ten cases hand-graded by the prompt's author against her own sense of quality.
A side-by-side comparison of a few outputs, with the team voting on the version they prefer.
A large set of automatically graded cases with measurable criteria, graded by a different model.
A large set graded by the same model that produced the outputs, since it knows the intent.

items.explanation: Anthropic's evaluation guidance says success criteria should be SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), that you should prioritise the volume of automatically graded questions over a small number of hand-graded ones, and that it is best practice to use a different model to grade an output than the model that generated it.

rationales.A: Ten hand-graded cases is exactly the low-volume, subjective pattern Anthropic advises against, and grading by the prompt's own author adds bias to an already small sample.
rationales.B: Preference voting over a handful of outputs gives neither volume nor measurable criteria, so it cannot show whether the change is a real improvement or noise.
rationales.D: Anthropic explicitly recommends a different model as grader. Self-grading is the documented anti-pattern because the generating model shares the blind spots being tested for.

items.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
items.stem: A support manager is writing a one-page triage card so first-line staff can distinguish normal Claude behaviour from a genuine fault. Select TWO statements that are accurate and belong on the card.

options.text: 'Due to unexpected capacity constraints' is normal load management and will not show on status.claude.com.
The banner '5-hour limit resets [time] - continuing with usage credits' means work has stopped until reset.
'Approaching 5-hour limit.' is a warning only; work continues until '5-hour limit reached' appears.
Any message not listed on status.claude.com should be escalated as a suspected unreported incident.
Claude Code and claude.ai hold separate allowances, so switching surface restores lost capacity.

items.explanation: Anthropic classifies the capacity-constraints message as high system-wide demand rather than an outage, with retry as the remedy and no status-page entry. The usage banners escalate in a documented order: 'Approaching 5-hour limit.' warns that the session ceiling is near, while '5-hour limit reached - resets [time].' is the message that blocks further work until the stated reset time.

rationales.B: This inverts the meaning. The 'continuing with usage credits' variant appears only when usage credits are enabled and signals that work continues on credits rather than stopping.
rationales.D: Most user-visible messages are normal behaviour and are deliberately absent from the status page. Escalating everything not listed there would flood the incident process with expected conditions.
rationales.E: Usage on claude.ai, Claude Desktop and Claude Code all counts against the same limit. They are not separate allowances.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: Which factors does Anthropic list as determining how quickly you consume your claude.ai usage limit?

options.text: Which surface is used, since Claude Code and claude.ai each meter their own allowance.
The number of conversations left open, the time of day, and how long the account has existed.
The number of Projects created and the total volume of files stored inside each Project.
Conversation length and complexity, the features used, the model selected, and the effort level.

items.explanation: Anthropic lists the usage-consuming factors as the length and complexity of conversations, the features used such as extended thinking, which Claude model is selected, and the effort level selected. It also states that usage on claude.ai, Claude Desktop and Claude Code all counts against the same limit.

rationales.A: This is the documented misconception. All three surfaces draw on the same limit, so surface choice does not change the allowance.
rationales.B: None of these is a documented factor. Usage is driven by what is processed and generated, not by open tabs, clock time or account age.
rationales.C: Content placed in a Project knowledge base is cached for reuse across conversations, so stored Project volume is not itself listed as a consumption driver.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: On the Pro plan, when does the weekly usage limit reset?

options.text: At a fixed time each week assigned to the account, which is shown in Settings > Usage.
Five hours after the session limit was last reached, in step with the session window.
On the monthly subscription anniversary date, alongside the billing cycle.
At midnight every Monday, expressed in the local time zone set on the account profile page.

items.explanation: The Pro plan has a session-based limit that resets every five hours plus a separate weekly limit that applies across all models. The weekly limit resets at a fixed time each week assigned to the individual account, and that time is visible in Settings > Usage.

rationales.B: That describes the separate 5-hour session window. The weekly limit is a distinct control that is not driven by session resets.
rationales.C: The weekly reset is deliberately decoupled from billing. Tying it to the subscription anniversary is a common misconception the documentation contradicts.
rationales.D: There is no universal Monday-midnight reset. Reset times are assigned per account so that load is spread, which is why the documentation points users to Settings > Usage.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A client-services consultant pastes the same 40-page delivery methodology into every new chat so Claude follows the house approach. She is hitting usage limits by Thursday most weeks. Which change is the MOST effective documented remedy?

options.text: Paste the methodology in smaller pieces spread over several messages in the same chat.
Upload the methodology once into a Project knowledge base and work inside that Project.
Buy a usage bundle so that the pasted methodology stops counting against her limits.
Keep a single very long running conversation so the methodology is only pasted once ever.

items.explanation: Anthropic's usage-limit best practices tell users to use project knowledge bases effectively, uploading documents to projects for caching benefits across multiple uses, and list projects with retrieval-augmented generation as a documented remedy for accounts that repeatedly hit limits. A single upload is cheaper than re-pasting the same material into every conversation.

rationales.A: Splitting the same content across several messages does not reduce what the conversation carries. Anthropic's guidance is to plan the conversation and provide background upfront so fewer messages are needed, not to drip-feed the same material.
rationales.C: Usage bundles supplement the plan after included usage is exhausted; they do not stop content from consuming usage, and they do not address the underlying repeated-content waste.
rationales.D: Anthropic recommends starting fresh conversations rather than extending lengthy ones, because longer conversations that trigger automatic context management consume more of your usage limit.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A team lead's analysts repeatedly reach the 5-hour usage limit by mid-afternoon and lose working time. Select TWO actions Anthropic documents for accounts that repeatedly hit usage limits.

options.text: Keep one long conversation open per analyst rather than starting new ones.
Turn off tools and connectors that are not needed for the work in hand.
Raise the maximum response length so fewer follow-up messages are needed.
Wait for the weekly limit to reset, which also clears the 5-hour session limit.
Have analysts sign in to Claude Desktop instead, which carries its own allowance.
Lower the effort level for routine tasks that do not need deep reasoning.

items.explanation: Anthropic's documented remedies for repeatedly hitting usage limits are to purchase usage credits, start fresh conversations rather than extending lengthy chats, use projects with retrieval-augmented generation, disable non-essential tools such as web search when they are not needed, and lower effort levels for routine tasks. Options A and B are two of those five.

rationales.A: The documented advice is the opposite: start fresh conversations rather than extending lengthy chats, because longer conversations that trigger automatic context management consume more of your usage limit.
rationales.C: A higher response ceiling does not reduce consumption; longer generated responses consume more, and the documented remedy for repeated follow-ups is to plan the conversation and provide background upfront.
rationales.D: The 5-hour session limit and the weekly limit are separate controls on their own reset cycles; the weekly reset does not clear the session window.
rationales.E: claude.ai, Claude Desktop and Claude Code all count against the same limit, so changing surface gains nothing.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: An operations analyst has been running one very long research conversation. It now responds slowly and has started missing details established earlier in the thread. A colleague tells her to 'just turn caching on'. Select TWO actions that would actually reduce the amount of context the work is carrying.

options.text: Start a fresh conversation and re-establish only the material still needed for the remaining work.
Move the core reference documents into a Project, where retrieval fetches only the relevant excerpts.
Move to a model with a larger nominal window, which prevents accuracy loss as tokens accumulate.
Enable prompt caching, which takes the cached material out of the context window.
Raise the maximum response length so more of the window becomes available to the conversation.

items.explanation: The documented context-bloat remedies include starting a new conversation and using Projects, where retrieval-augmented generation activates automatically once knowledge approaches the context limit and Claude fetches only relevant excerpts through the project knowledge search tool. Both genuinely reduce how much material is being carried.

rationales.C: A larger window delays the hard limit but does not prevent context rot, the documented degradation of accuracy and recall as token count grows. Anthropic states that more context is not automatically better.
rationales.D: This is the classic trap. Prompt caching changes what you pay for tokens, not whether they occupy the window; cached prefixes still consume the full context space.
rationales.E: Raising the response ceiling changes how much Claude may generate. It removes nothing from the material the conversation is already carrying, so it does not reduce context at all.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A marketing manager wants her team to get more out of the same plan without upgrading. Select THREE practices that Anthropic publishes as ways to stretch usage.

options.text: Ask Claude to restate the earlier context at the start of each new message so nothing is lost.
Batch similar requests into a single message instead of sending them one at a time.
Raise the effort level on routine drafting so that fewer revision rounds are needed.
Review and edit a prompt before sending it rather than correcting it over several turns.
Split every task across several short chats so each one stays well under the length limit.
Provide the complete material in the first message rather than adding it turn by turn.

items.explanation: Anthropic's published usage-stretching practices include starting by planning your conversations, being specific and concise, using chat search and memory instead of repeating information, batching similar requests in one message, reviewing and editing your prompt before sending, using project knowledge bases effectively, and monitoring consumption in Usage settings. Planning the conversation explicitly means considering what you need before messaging, combining related questions and providing background upfront, which reduces the number of back-and-forth messages needed.

rationales.A: Restating context deliberately duplicates tokens every turn. Anthropic's guidance is the opposite: lean on chat search and memory rather than repeating information.
rationales.C: Effort level is one of the factors that drives consumption, and Anthropic's documented advice is to lower effort for routine tasks, not raise it.
rationales.E: Fragmenting work forces the same context to be re-supplied in each chat. The documented pattern is to plan the conversation and provide background upfront, not to split tasks by default.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A team lead cannot tell what is driving her team through its allowance so quickly, and wants the conversation with them to rest on data rather than guesswork. Which documented step gives her that data?

options.text: Ask Claude at the end of each chat to report how much of the allowance that chat used.
Read the monthly invoice, which itemises consumption by conversation and by feature.
Open Settings > Usage and review consumption against the session and weekly limits.
Check status.claude.com, which publishes per-account consumption alongside any incidents.

items.explanation: Anthropic's usage-limit best practices include monitoring your consumption in Usage settings, tracking session and weekly limits through the Settings > Usage dashboard, and the Pro plan documentation points users to the same place for the fixed weekly reset time assigned to their account. Consumption is driven by conversation length and complexity, the features used, the model selected and the effort level, so the dashboard is the documented place to see what is actually being spent.

rationales.A: Claude has no access to the account's usage metering, and a self-reported figure is not a documented source of consumption data.
rationales.B: Billing documents cover the subscription, not per-conversation or per-feature consumption. The documented monitoring surface is Settings > Usage.
rationales.D: status.claude.com publishes service incidents. It carries no account-level information of any kind, so it cannot show what the team is consuming.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A team lead runs long working sessions in claude.ai and has code execution enabled. Someone on the team worries that once a conversation approaches the context window limit, earlier turns will be lost. What actually happens?

options.text: It permanently deletes the oldest messages from the chat so that newer turns have room to continue.
It pauses the conversation until additional usage credits are purchased to extend the context window.
It locks the conversation, which must then be exported before any further messages can be sent in it.
Claude summarises earlier messages so the conversation can continue, and the full history stays viewable.

items.explanation: Anthropic's usage and length limits article states that Claude summarises earlier messages to continue the conversation seamlessly, and that code execution must be enabled for this automatic context management. Earlier turns are condensed rather than deleted, and the full history remains viewable. Note that conversations which trigger automatic context management consume more of the usage limit, so starting a fresh conversation can still be the better move.

rationales.A: Nothing is deleted. Earlier messages are summarised for the model's working context while the full history remains accessible to the user.
rationales.B: Usage credits relate to usage limits, which are a separate control from the context window. The conversation is not held pending a purchase; it continues through summarisation.
rationales.C: There is no lock-and-export step. Automatic context management is designed specifically so the conversation can keep going.

items.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
items.stem: A Pro subscriber purchases a usage bundle. What does that bundle actually provide?

options.text: Pre-purchased credits that are drawn on only once the plan's included usage is exhausted.
A separate allowance reserved for Claude Code that leaves claude.ai usage untouched.
A higher 5-hour and weekly limit for the remainder of the current billing period.
Removal of the per-chat length limit, so that long conversations run without interruption.

items.explanation: Usage bundles are pre-purchased usage credits, sold at a discount, that activate only after the plan's included usage is exhausted. The balance is shared across Claude, Claude Desktop, Claude Mobile, Claude Code and Cowork rather than being reserved for one surface.

rationales.B: The credit balance is shared across all Claude surfaces. Nothing about a bundle ring-fences capacity for a single product.
rationales.C: Credits supplement the plan rather than raising the 5-hour or weekly limits. The limits themselves are unchanged; credits simply let work continue past them.
rationales.D: The per-chat length limit is a context-length constraint, not a usage constraint, so credits have no effect on it.
